title: The Ramayana
invocationMantra: श्री राम जय राम जय जय राम
subtitle: Seven books, one exile, and an ending that has troubled readers for two thousand years

तपःस्वाध्यायनिरतं तपस्वी वाग्विदां वरम् ।
नारदं परिपप्रच्छ वाल्मीकिर्मुनिपुङ्गवम् ॥
invocation.translation:
tapaḥsvādhyāyanirataṁ tapasvī vāgvidāṁ varam | nāradaṁ paripapraccha vālmīkir munipuṅgavam ||
"Vālmīki the ascetic put a question to Nārada — bull among sages, devoted to austerity and to recitation, finest of those who know speech." — Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla Kāṇḍa 1.1. The poem does not open with an answer. It opens with a man asking someone else a question.

sections.label: Orientation
sections.title: Before We Begin
sections.subtitle: There is no such thing as the Ramayana — and understanding why is the first real thing this course can give you

blocks.html: Somewhere in Karnataka, women have told a story about the Ramayana that goes like this. Rama's signet ring slips from his hand and falls through a hole in the floor. He sends Hanuman down after it. Hanuman shrinks, drops through the hole, and lands in the netherworld, where the king of spirits is waiting for him — and beside the king is a platter heaped with thousands of identical rings. Take yours, the king says. But which is mine? asks Hanuman. And the king tells him: every time a Rama is about to end his life on earth, his ring falls, and one of my agents brings it here. There have been as many Ramas as there are rings on that platter. Go up if you like — the Rama you came from will already be gone.

blocks.name: lenses
blocks.caption: Three kinds of true, kept apart — which matters more here than anywhere else in the library.

blocks.html: A. K. Ramanujan collected that folktale, and he put it near the centre of the most useful essay ever written about this material. It is a story that a tradition tells about itself, and what it says is startling: the Ramayana has happened many times, in many worlds, and no telling of it is the only one. That is not a modern academic's mischief imported into a devotional text. It is the folk tradition's own theology of its own multiplicity.

So let us begin with the fact that everything else in this course depends on. There is no single Ramayana. There is a family of Ramayanas — hundreds of them, in dozens of languages, across at least a dozen cultures, some of them agreeing on almost nothing except a set of names. If you have grown up with one, this can feel like an attack. It is the opposite. It is the reason the story is still alive.
Three Hundred Ramayanas

In 1987 the poet and scholar A. K. Ramanujan gave a paper called "Three Hundred Rāmāyaṇas: Five Examples and Three Thoughts on Translation," published a few years later in Paula Richman's volume Many Rāmāyaṇas (University of California Press, 1991). The number in his title is not his own. He took it from the Belgian-Indian scholar Camille Bulcke, a Jesuit who spent his working life in Ranchi writing Hindi and counting Rama-stories, and whose survey Rāmakathā tallied something on the order of three hundred distinct tellings. Ramanujan's own view was that the true number, if you counted the oral and performance traditions properly, would be very much larger.

Ramanujan made one terminological choice that does most of the work of the essay. He refused the word version, and he refused variant even more firmly, because both smuggle in an assumption: that somewhere there is an original of which the others are deviations. He used "tellings." A telling is not a corruption of anything. Kamban in Tamil was not producing a flawed copy of Valmiki; he was doing in Tamil, for a Tamil audience, in the twelfth century, what Valmiki had done in Sanskrit a millennium or more earlier. His picture of the whole field was of a common pool of names, situations and images — a lexicon — from which each poet, each singer, each puppeteer draws to make a new sentence.

blocks.tag: Historical Lens · An Essay That Was Withdrawn

blocks.html: It is worth knowing that this is not a settled or comfortable position. Ramanujan's essay was prescribed reading in the BA History syllabus at the University of Delhi. In 2008 the university's history department office was vandalised by activists objecting to it; in October 2011, after a long dispute and a vote in the Academic Council, the essay was removed from the syllabus, over the objection of the majority of the expert committee the university had itself convened. A large number of Indian and international scholars protested the decision publicly.

I mention this at the very start not to score a point but as a fact about the terrain. The multiplicity of the Ramayana is not an obscure scholarly hobby. It is, for some readers, a live and painful question — because a story that has been told three hundred ways cannot easily be made to say one thing, and there are people who need it to say one thing. This course will not pretend that difficulty away.
What Valmiki Is, and What Valmiki Is Not

Against all of that, one text still has a special place, and this course will spend most of its length inside it. The Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa is the oldest surviving Rama-story in Sanskrit, and it is the one from which an enormous amount — though by no means all — of the later tradition took its bearings. Four precise claims, and it matters that you can tell them apart:

items: It is the oldest surviving Sanskrit telling. True, and not seriously disputed. That is a statement about what has come down to us, not about what once existed.

It is the original from which all others derive. False, or at least far too strong. The Buddhist Dasaratha Jātaka in Pali and the Jain Paümacariya in Prakrit tell the story in ways that do not look like edits of Valmiki's poem, and both traditions explicitly claim to be correcting a false account rather than adapting a true one. Many folk tellings appear to draw on a shared stock of episodes rather than on the Sanskrit text.

It is a single fixed text. False. Valmiki's poem itself survives in two great families of manuscripts, Northern and Southern, which differ from one another substantially — in wording, in order, and in whole passages present in one and absent in the other. The text you are handed in a bookshop is an edited object.

It is one man's composition. Almost certainly not, at least not the text we have. Book One and Book Seven of the seven are held by most scholars to be later than the rest, and material has demonstrably been added throughout. We will look at the evidence for that in a moment, and at what it does and does not license you to conclude.

blocks.html: A word on the word kāvya. The tradition calls this poem the ādikāvya, the first poem — meaning the first work of deliberate literary art, as distinct from the Veda, which was heard rather than made. Valmiki is the ādikavi, the first poet. Whether or not that is historically accurate, it is a precise piece of self-understanding: the tradition knew the difference between revelation and authorship, and placed this text firmly on the authored side.
The Three Lenses

One promise before we start, and it is the whole method of this library. There are three completely different ways of speaking truthfully about a text like this, and I will never let one impersonate another. On a text as contested as this one, that discipline is not fussiness. It is the only thing that keeps the course usable by a devotee and a historian at the same time.

items.title: Scriptural
items.html: What the poem actually says, in the passage, in its own idiom — including the parts nobody quotes. When I tell you Rama says something cold to Sita after the war, I will tell you where, and I will not soften it. When I tell you Vali accuses Rama of murder, that accusation is in the text, put in Vali's mouth by the poet.

items.title: Symbolic / Philosophical
items.html: What the tradition has understood these events to mean — the commentators, the bhakti poets, the Advaitin reading of Rama as Brahman, the reading of Sita's fire as her return from Agni's safekeeping. A reading is not a forgery. But a reading is also not the text, and when a reading exists mainly to remove a difficulty, I will say so.

items.title: Historical / Scholarly
items.html: What manuscripts, linguistics, archaeology and geology can establish: when the layers were composed, which passages the critical editors judged to be insertions, what is actually at the bottom of the Palk Strait. Probabilistic, revisable, stated with its error bars showing, and silent where it has nothing to say.

blocks.html: The failure mode on one side is to dress history in scripture's clothes — the Pushpaka was a jet aircraft, the setu was an engineered causeway, here is the date of Rama's birth to the day. The failure mode on the other side is to dress contempt in history's clothes — it is a feudal fantasy and a caste manual, and there is nothing else in it. Both mistakes come from the same place: an inability to let a work of literature be a work of literature, doing what literature does, for three thousand years, to hundreds of millions of people.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · The Question the Poem Begins With
blocks.sk:
को न्वस्मिन्साम्प्रतं लोके गुणवान्कश्च वीर्यवान् ।
धर्मज्ञश्च कृतज्ञश्च सत्यवाक्यो दृढव्रतः ॥
blocks.tr:
ko nv asmin sāmprataṁ loke guṇavān kaś ca vīryavān |
dharmajñaś ca kṛtajñaś ca satyavākyo dṛḍhavrataḥ ||
blocks.mn: "Who is there in the world at present who is a man of quality and also strong — one who knows dharma and remembers a kindness, whose word is true, whose vow is firm?"
blocks.src: — Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla Kāṇḍa 1.2 (sarga and verse numbering differs between recensions)

blocks.html: That is Valmiki asking Narada, in the second verse of the poem. Read it once more and notice its form. It is not a proposition, it is an enquiry — and specifically an enquiry about whether a certain kind of person can exist at all. The whole epic is the answer, and the last book is where the poem itself begins to doubt the answer it gave. If you keep hold of nothing else from this orientation, keep that: this is a poem about whether perfect conduct is possible, written by someone who was not sure.
How This Course Moves

Five parts. First, the poem — its extraordinary origin story, and the shape of its seven books, including the scholarly account of which parts are late and why. Then the seven books themselves, one section each, told as narrative, because you cannot argue about a story you do not know. Then the hard questions: the fire ordeal and the banishment of Sita, the killing of Vali from concealment, the killing of Shambuka, and the strange dignity the poem gives to Ravana. I am not going to be delicate there; that part is the most valuable thing in this course and being delicate would ruin it. Then the many Ramayanas — Tamil, Awadhi, Prakrit, Pali, Bengali, Telugu, Thai, Javanese, and the women's songs that most anthologies leave out. And then the honest ending, where we test the loud modern claims against evidence, and finish quietly.

blocks.tag: Reflect

blocks.html: Before you read on, write down the Ramayana as you currently hold it — not a summary, but the shape of it: where it begins, where it ends, who the story is about, and what it is finally saying. One paragraph. Be honest about the gaps; if you are not sure what happens in Book Seven, write that down too.

Keep the page. Almost everyone who does this discovers at the end that they were carrying one particular telling and mistaking it for the whole thing — usually a telling that ends about eighty percent of the way through the Sanskrit text. That discovery is not a loss. It is the beginning of actually having the thing.

sections.label: Chapter 01 · Origins
sections.title: The Hunter and the Birds
sections.subtitle: How a curse spoken over a dead crane became the first metre of Sanskrit poetry

blocks.html: Every literature has a story about where poetry comes from. Most of them are boring. This one is not, and it deserves to be told slowly, because it is one of the great self-descriptions in world literature — a tradition explaining, in a single scene lasting perhaps ninety seconds, what it thinks a poem is.

It is in the second sarga of the Bala Kanda. Valmiki has just heard from the sage Narada a compressed summary of the whole story of Rama — a hundred verses of plot, delivered like a report. Then Narada leaves. And Valmiki, with his pupil Bharadvaja, walks down to the river Tamasa to bathe.

The poem takes its time here in a way it rarely does. Valmiki looks at the water and remarks on how clear it is — unmuddied, he says, like the mind of a good man. Then he sets down his bark garment and looks about the wood. And in the branches he sees a pair of krauñca birds, cranes, calling to each other, entirely absorbed in one another and in nothing else.

A Nishada — a forest hunter — shoots the male. It falls to the ground, thrashing, covered in blood. The female circles it, crying a particular cry that the poem describes in detail: she has seen its wings smeared, its body writhing on the earth, and she wails.

And something happens to Valmiki that he does not choose. The text is careful about this. It says compassion arose in him — karuṇa — and then, out of that state and not out of any intention to compose, speech came out of his mouth in a shape it had never had before:

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · The First Śloka
blocks.sk:
मा निषाद प्रतिष्ठां त्वमगमः शाश्वतीः समाः ।
यत्क्रौञ्चमिथुनादेकमवधीः काममोहितम् ॥
blocks.tr:
mā niṣāda pratiṣṭhāṁ tvam agamaḥ śāśvatīḥ samāḥ |
yat krauñcamithunād ekam avadhīḥ kāmamohitam ||
blocks.mn: "Hunter — may you never in all your endless years find rest, since you killed one of a pair of cranes lost in love."
blocks.src: — Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Bāla Kāṇḍa, sarga 2 (2.15 in the common southern numbering)

blocks.html: Then comes the part that makes this more than a pretty legend. Valmiki stands there and examines what has just come out of him. He notices that it has four quarters, that the quarters have equal syllables, that it could be sung to the beat of a stringed instrument. He is astonished. And he says to his pupil, more or less: whatever this was that came out of me while I was in grief, let it be called śloka and nothing else.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · Valmiki Names the Metre
blocks.sk:
पादबद्धोऽक्षरसमस्तन्त्रीलयसमन्वितः ।
शोकार्तस्य प्रवृत्तो मे श्लोको भवतु नान्यथा ॥
blocks.tr:
pādabaddho 'kṣarasamas tantrīlayasamanvitaḥ |
śokārtasya pravṛtto me śloko bhavatu nānyathā ||
blocks.mn: "Bound into quarters, equal in syllables, fitted to the rhythm of the lyre — since it issued from me in my grief, let it be śloka, and nothing else."

blocks.html: Śoka Becomes Śloka

The pun is the point, and it is untranslatable, so hold the two words next to each other. śoka (शोक) is grief — the ordinary, unliterary word for what you feel at a funeral. śloka (श्लोक) is the verse, the couplet of thirty-two syllables in which almost all Sanskrit narrative poetry, including the entire Ramayana and the entire Mahabharata, would afterwards be composed. One consonant apart. The tradition's claim is not that grief is a subject of poetry. It is that metre itself is what grief does when it has nowhere else to go.

Notice also what the first poem in Sanskrit literature actually is, on its own terms. It is not a hymn. It is not praise. It is not addressed to a god. It is a curse spoken to a working man by someone who has just watched an animal die, and it is spoken on behalf of the surviving bird. The founding act of this literature is an act of grief on behalf of a creature that cannot speak for itself.

blocks.tag: Symbolic Lens · Two Readings the Tradition Made of This Verse

blocks.html: First: the double meaning. The commentators noticed that mā can be read not as the negative particle ("may you not") but as a name of Śrī, the goddess. Read that way, the same syllables become a blessing addressed to Vishnu: O you in whom Śrī dwells, may you attain everlasting glory, because you killed one of the pair of demons deluded by lust. The first verse of the poem, read a second time, is a prophecy of Rama killing Ravana. Whether Valmiki intended this is unanswerable and beside the point; what it tells you is how the tradition reads — as though every surface has another surface under it.

Second: the theory of poetry. Sanskrit aesthetics took this episode as its foundational case study. The Kashmiri theorist Ānandavardhana, writing the Dhvanyāloka in the ninth century, uses the birth of the śloka from Valmiki's grief as a model instance of how a work of art carries an emotional content that is suggested rather than stated — the doctrine of dhvani, resonance, which became the dominant theory of literature in India for the next thousand years. Indian poetics did not begin by asking what a poem means. It began by asking what a poem does to the person it goes through.
Brahma's Commission

Valmiki goes back to his hermitage, still turning the thing over, half-embarrassed by it. And Brahma arrives — the creator, seated, unannounced — and tells him two things. The first is that the verse came out of him by Brahma's will; he need not be puzzled about it. The second is an instruction: compose the entire story of Rama in this metre. Whatever you do not know of it, Brahma says, will become known to you; nothing in your poem will be untrue.

And then a promise that has been quoted for two thousand years and has, in a plain empirical sense, come true: as long as the mountains and the rivers remain on the earth, the story of the Ramayana will circulate in the worlds.

So Valmiki composes it — and here the poem gives its own dimensions, which we will need later: twenty-four thousand verses, five hundred sargas, in seven books. Then he teaches it to two boys living in his hermitage, Kusha and Lava, who have beautiful voices and prodigious memories. They learn to sing it. They sing it in the assemblies of sages, and then in the streets, and eventually — the poem's most audacious move — they sing it in the court of King Rama himself, who listens to the whole of his own life, does not at first recognise the singers, and only slowly understands who they are and who their mother is.

blocks.tag: Story · The Shape of the Frame

blocks.html: Sit with the architecture for a second, because it is very strange. The Ramayana contains, inside itself, a scene in which the Ramayana is performed. The performers are Rama's own sons, whom he has never met, born in the forest to the wife he sent away. The audience is Rama. The subject is Rama. And the passage of the poem that Rama is hearing, at the moment the story reaches him, includes the part where he sends his wife into the forest.

There are perhaps four or five moments in world literature of this order of self-reference, and this is one of the oldest. A poem that folds back on itself in this way is not a naive text, whatever else it is.
What the Historian Has to Say About This
Now the other lens, and it neither confirms nor destroys the story — it relocates it.

The śloka metre was not invented in that clearing. It is a development of the Vedic anuṣṭubh, a stanza of four eight-syllable quarters that occurs in the Rigveda itself, centuries before any plausible date for Valmiki. What changed between the Vedic anuṣṭubh and the epic śloka is a hardening of the rhythmic rules at the end of each quarter — a technical development, traceable, and gradual. Nobody woke it up by the side of a river.

So the origin story is false as chronology. But look at what it is actually claiming, and it turns out not to be a claim about chronology at all. It is a claim about genre. Before this, Sanskrit verse in this metre was liturgical: it addressed gods, it accompanied ritual, it was śruti, heard rather than made. What begins here is something different — extended narrative poetry about human beings, composed by a named author, whose subject is what happens to people and what they feel about it. On that claim the tradition is exactly right, and it knew it, which is why it called this text the ādikāvya: not the first verse, the first poem.

blocks.tag: Reflect · The Arrow, Again

blocks.html: Readers have noticed for a long time — and you are entitled to notice it too — that the image the poem opens with does not stay in the opening. A pair of creatures absorbed in each other; an arrow from outside; one of them taken; the other left circling and crying. That is the Ramayana. It is what happens to Rama and Sita in the forest, and it is what happens to them again at the end, when the arrow is Rama's own decision.

And there is a harder echo still. The hunter kills from concealment, at a creature that is not looking at him. In Book Four, Rama will do exactly that to Vali. The poem does not comment on the resemblance. Whether it is design or accident, it is there in the text, and once you have seen it you cannot stop seeing it.

sections.label: Chapter 02 · Structure
sections.title: Seven Books
sections.subtitle: The architecture of the poem, and the strong scholarly case that the first and last of its books were added later

blocks.html: The Ramayana is divided into seven kāṇḍas — the word means a section, a joint, a length of stalk between two nodes, which is a good image for what they are. Each is a self-contained movement with its own tempo, and readers who love the poem tend to love particular books rather than the whole, in the way that people love particular movements of a symphony.
Here is the whole thing in one view. Read this table once now, without trying to memorise it, and then come back to it whenever you lose your bearings in Part Two.

head: Book
The name
What happens
Character and scale
rows: The frame: Valmiki, the cranes, Brahma, Kusha and Lava. Then Dasharatha's sacrifice for sons; the birth of Rama, Bharata, Lakshmana and Shatrughna; Vishvamitra taking the boys to guard a sacrifice; the killing of Tataka; Ahalya; the breaking of Shiva's bow at Mithila; the four weddings; the encounter with Parashurama on the road home.

Around 77 sargas. Episodic and anthological — it carries a great many inset legends (the descent of the Ganga, the churning of the ocean) that have little to do with Rama. Widely regarded as later than the core.

The consecration announced; Manthara and Kaikeyi; the two boons; Rama's exile; Sita and Lakshmana insisting on going; the departure and the city's grief; Guha the Nishada; Chitrakuta; Dasharatha's death and the story of the blind couple's son; Bharata's refusal of the throne; the sandals; Nandigrama.
Around 119 sargas — the longest book after the war. No demons, no magic, almost no fighting. It is domestic tragedy at full strength, and many readers consider it the finest thing in the poem.

Thirteen years in the deep forest; the sages' appeal; Sita's argument against carrying weapons; Shurpanakha and her mutilation; Khara and Dushana; Maricha as the golden deer; the abduction; Jatayu's death; Shabari; the first news of Sugriva.
Around 75 sargas. The tone changes completely — wilderness, monsters, sudden violence. The hinge of the whole epic falls here.

Hanuman's first meeting with Rama; the alliance with Sugriva; the killing of Vali from concealment; Tara's lament; the rains on Prasravana and Rama's despair; Lakshmana's fury; the search parties sent to the four directions; Sampati; Hanuman persuaded of his own strength on the southern shore.
Around 67 sargas. A political book — usurpation, alliance, obligation, delay — with the epic's most extended passage of pure landscape writing in the monsoon chapters.

Hanuman alone: the leap across the ocean, Mainaka, Surasa, Simhika; the search through Lanka by night; Sita found beneath the shinshapa tree; the conversation; the ring; the destruction of the grove; capture, the audience with Ravana, the burning tail, the burning of Lanka; the return with news.
Around 68 sargas. The one book routinely recited on its own, as a complete devotional act. Single protagonist, single continuous action, and the only book in which nothing is lost.

Vibhishana's defection and Rama's promise of refuge; the bridge; the siege; Kumbhakarna; Indrajit and the serpent-arrows; the healing herbs; the death of Ravana; the funeral rites; the fire ordeal; the flight home; the coronation.
Around 128 sargas — the longest book. Vast, repetitive, formulaic in the way battle poetry everywhere is, and then suddenly, in its last few chapters, devastating.

Ravana's ancestry and career told in retrospect, including the curse that prevents him forcing a woman; Hanuman's childhood; then the rumour in the city, the banishment of the pregnant Sita, Valmiki's hermitage, the birth of Lava and Kusha; Shambuka; the horse sacrifice; Sita's oath and her return to the earth; the departure of Lakshmana; and Rama walking into the Sarayu.
Around 111 sargas. Loose, Puranic, episodic — and it contains the two passages that have caused more anguish and more argument than everything else in the epic combined.

blocks.html: Sarga counts differ between recensions and even between printed editions, so treat the numbers above as approximate. And note a detail worth carrying: the poem describes itself as having 500 sargas and 24,000 verses. Count the sargas in any printed Valmiki and you will get somewhere north of 640. The text has outgrown its own description of itself — which is not a scandal, but it is a clue.
The Case That Books One and Seven Are Later
This is the single most useful piece of scholarship you can carry into a reading of the Ramayana, so let us take it slowly and let us be careful about what it does and does not prove.

The argument was made systematically by the German Indologist Hermann Jacobi in Das Rāmāyaṇa (1893), and although details have been argued over ever since, the core of it has held up and is now the ordinary working assumption of the field. The most thorough modern treatment is John Brockington's Righteous Rāma: The Evolution of an Epic (1984) and his later The Sanskrit Epics (1998), which divide the growth of the text into stages. The evidence is of several independent kinds, and it is the convergence that makes it strong:

items: The poem ends twice. Book Six closes with a phalaśruti — the traditional passage listing the benefits of having heard the work — which is the standard way a completed Sanskrit text signs off. Then Book Seven begins. A text that says goodbye and then keeps talking is telling you something about its own history.

Rama's divinity is unevenly distributed. Through most of Books Two to Six, Rama behaves and is treated as a man: he grieves uncontrollably, he despairs, he makes mistakes, other characters address him as a prince. The explicit machinery of avatāra — Vishnu agreeing to be born, the gods arranging matters, Brahma announcing at the end that Rama is Vishnu — is concentrated in Books One and Seven, plus a small number of passages elsewhere that stand out from their surroundings. That is exactly the pattern you would expect if a heroic poem about a man was later given a theological frame.

Book One duplicates and anticipates. It gives the whole plot twice over in summary before starting, and its long inset stories — the Ganga's descent, the churning of the ocean, the Vishvamitra–Vasishtha feud — read as anthology material attached to the front of an existing poem.

Book Seven is not the same kind of writing. Its manner is Puranic rather than epic: genealogies, cosmological back-story, a chain of separable episodes. Its Sanskrit and its narrative habits differ measurably from the core books.

Narada's summary does not cover it. The compressed retelling that Narada gives Valmiki in the first sarga runs to Rama's reign and the peace of his kingdom. The material that makes Book Seven unbearable — the banishment, Sita's death, the killing of Shambuka — is not in the summary of the poem that the poem gives of itself.

blocks.tag: Historical Lens · What This Argument Is Not

blocks.html: Three cautions, and they will matter enormously in Part Three.

It is not a claim that the core is pristine. Books Two to Six have also grown. Material has been added inside them — including, by many readers' judgement, some of the theological passages in the war book. "Core" means older, not original.

It is not a dating of Book Seven to yesterday. Whenever the Uttara Kanda was added, it was early enough that it appears in both the Northern and Southern recensions and has been part of every complete manuscript tradition we have. We are talking about a text that has been in the Ramayana for something on the order of two thousand years.

And it is not an eraser. This is the caution that gets forgotten. Establishing that a passage is a later stratum is a statement about textual history. It does not remove the passage from the tradition, from the manuscripts, from the temples, or from the minds of the people who have grown up with it. We will come back to this, hard, when we reach Sita's banishment.
Which Text, Exactly?
One more piece of apparatus and then we can begin the story. When someone says "Valmiki's Ramayana," they may mean one of several different objects.

The manuscripts fall into two large families, conventionally the Northern (itself splitting into north-western and north-eastern) and the Southern. They are not trivially different. Whole passages appear in one and not the other; the order of episodes shifts; individual verses differ constantly. The printed "vulgate" familiar in India, with the great southern commentaries attached to it, runs to roughly twenty-four thousand verses.

Between 1960 and 1975 the Oriental Institute at Baroda published the Critical Edition — seven volumes, begun under G. H. Bhatt and completed under U. P. Shah, constituted by comparing a large body of manuscripts from every region and reconstructing, verse by verse, what the editors judged to be the earliest recoverable text. It is shorter than the vulgate by several thousand verses. Everything the editors set aside is still printed, in the apparatus, where anyone can inspect the decision.

In English, the standard scholarly translation is the seven-volume Princeton Rāmāyaṇa of Vālmīki: An Epic of Ancient India, under the general editorship of Robert P. Goldman, begun in 1984 and completed in 2017 with the Uttara Kanda translated by Robert and Sally Sutherland Goldman. It follows the critical edition, and its introductions and notes are where an English reader can actually see the scholarship arguing with itself.

Throughout this course, when I cite a chapter and verse I am giving the commonly used southern numbering, because that is what most readers will have in front of them. Numbering in the critical edition differs, sometimes by several sargas. Where a passage's authenticity is contested, I will say so at the point where it matters rather than burying it in a footnote.
॥ श्री राम ॥

sections.label: Book One · Bāla Kāṇḍa
sections.title: The Book of Childhood
sections.subtitle: A childless king, a loophole in a demon's boon, and a bow that nobody can lift

blocks.html: Book One is the book with the most famous incidents and the least narrative pressure. It is where the marriage happens, where the bow breaks, where Ahalya is released — scenes every Indian child knows — and it is also the book that scholars are most confident was assembled after the rest. Both of those things are true at once, and they explain each other: material accretes around a story at the places where the story leaves room.
The Loophole
The whole plot of the Ramayana turns on a piece of carelessness in the wording of a boon, and Book One is where we are told about it.

Ravana, king of the rakshasas in Lanka, has performed austerities of terrifying severity and been granted by Brahma that he cannot be killed by gods, or danavas, or gandharvas, or yakshas, or rakshasas. He listed everything he considered a threat. He did not trouble to include human beings, or animals — beneath his notice. So when the gods come to Vishnu, unable to act against him, the answer is fixed by grammar: Ravana can be killed by a man. Vishnu agrees to be born as one, and to be helped by the second category Ravana forgot, the forest creatures.

This is a good place to notice the shape of the theology. The gods in this poem are not omnipotent; they are bound by their own word, which is exactly why boons are dangerous and exactly why Dasharatha, later, cannot take back a promise made to a wife in bed after a battle. A universe in which a spoken word binds even Brahma is a universe in which Kaikeyi's two boons are unanswerable. The epic is consistent about this from beginning to end.
The Sacrifice for Sons

In Ayodhya, King Dasharatha of the Ikshvaku line has three queens — Kausalya, Kaikeyi, Sumitra — and no children, and he is growing old. He performs a horse sacrifice and then a further rite for the obtaining of sons, conducted by the sage Rishyashringa, whose own story (a boy raised in the forest who has never seen a woman, brought to a drought-stricken kingdom by courtesans) the poem tells at length and with obvious enjoyment.

From the sacrificial fire a being rises holding a vessel of pāyasa — rice cooked in milk — and tells Dasharatha to give it to his wives. He divides it between them. Four sons are born: Rama to Kausalya, Bharata to Kaikeyi, and the twins Lakshmana and Shatrughna to Sumitra. The pairing that will govern the rest of the poem is set from birth: Lakshmana attaches himself to Rama, Shatrughna to Bharata, in a way the text treats as constitutional rather than chosen.
Vishvamitra Takes the Boys

The sage Vishvamitra arrives at court and asks for Rama — a boy of about sixteen — to protect his sacrifice from rakshasas who defile it. Dasharatha, who has just spent decades acquiring this child, offers his whole army instead and is refused. Vasishtha, the family priest, tells him to let the boy go.
On the road, three things happen that are worth marking.

items: Tataka. Vishvamitra orders Rama to kill a rakshasi who has made a wasteland of the region. Rama hesitates — she is a woman — and Vishvamitra has to argue him into it, citing precedents and the principle that a king's duty to protect his people overrides scruple. It is the first ethical argument in the poem and it is worth noticing that Rama loses it. This pattern, in which Rama does something questionable and the poem supplies a justification afterwards, will recur.

The weapons. Vishvamitra teaches him the mantras balā and atibalā, which remove hunger, thirst and fatigue, and then transmits the divine weapons — the astras — which in this poem are not objects but formulas: they are invoked, they come, they are dismissed by name.
Ahalya. On the way to Mithila they pass an abandoned hermitage where Rama's arrival releases the sage Gautama's wife from a curse.

blocks.tag: Scriptural Lens · What Valmiki Actually Says About Ahalya

blocks.html: This is a good early test of whether you are reading the text or the tradition. In the version most people know, Indra deceives Ahalya by taking her husband's form, she is innocent, and Gautama turns her to stone; Rama's foot restores her.

Valmiki's account differs on both counts. Indra does come in Gautama's form — but the text says Ahalya knew who he was, and consented, out of curiosity about the king of the gods. And she is not turned to stone. Gautama's curse condemns her to remain in that hermitage for thousands of years, invisible, living on air, lying in ashes, unseen by any creature, until Rama comes; and Indra is punished separately and severely. When Rama arrives she becomes visible again, is honoured, and returns to her husband.

The stone, and Ahalya's innocence, belong to the later retellings — where they do real work, because a tradition that increasingly wanted its women blameless had to do something about a text that had not made her so. Neither version is a forgery. But if someone tells you "in the Ramayana, Ahalya was turned to stone," the accurate reply is: in which Ramayana?
Mithila, and the Bow

At Mithila reigns Janaka, a king the tradition remembers as a philosopher — he appears in the Upanishads holding debates. He has in his possession an enormous bow, once Shiva's, which is kept on a cart because no one can move it. And he has a daughter.

She was not born to him. Ploughing a field for a sacrifice, he turned up a child in the furrow and raised her as his own. The Sanskrit word for that furrow is sītā (सीता), and it is her name. She is ayonijā, not born from a womb; her mother, in the plain sense of the story, is the earth. Remember this. It is the hinge on which the last scene of the whole poem will turn, four books and a lifetime later.

Janaka has sworn to give Sita to whoever can string the bow. Rama lifts it, bends it, and it breaks with a sound like thunder. Four weddings follow: Rama and Sita, Lakshmana and Urmila, Bharata and Mandavi, Shatrughna and Shrutakirti. On the road home the party is stopped by Parashurama, the axe-bearing brahmin destroyer of kshatriyas, who is contemptuous about the broken bow and produces a greater one; Rama strings it effortlessly, and Parashurama withdraws, diminished. It is the poem's way of saying, without saying it, that the age has changed hands.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · Vishvamitra Wakes Rama
blocks.sk:
कौसल्या सुप्रजा राम पूर्वा सन्ध्या प्रवर्तते ।
उत्तिष्ठ नरशार्दूल कर्तव्यं दैवमाह्निकम् ॥
blocks.tr:
kausalyā suprajā rāma pūrvā sandhyā pravartate |
uttiṣṭha naraśārdūla kartavyaṁ daivam āhnikam ||
blocks.mn: "Rama — Kausalya is blessed in such a son. The eastern twilight is coming on. Get up, tiger among men: the morning observances must be done."

blocks.html: That line has had an afterlife out of all proportion to its place in the story. It is the opening verse of the Veṅkaṭeśa Suprabhātam, sung at the Tirumala temple before dawn and broadcast into millions of houses every morning across south India. A sage waking a teenage boy for his prayers, in a poem about something else entirely, has become the sound of daybreak for an entire region.

blocks.tag: Historical Lens · Why This Book Reads Like an Anthology

blocks.html: Read the Bala Kanda straight through and you will feel the thing that made scholars suspicious. The narrative keeps stopping so that someone can tell a long story about something else: how the Ganga came down to earth, how the gods and demons churned the ocean, how Vishvamitra ceased to be a king and became a brahmarshi through several lifetimes of effort and failure. These are magnificent, and several of them are the standard versions of those myths in Indian literature. They also have essentially nothing to do with Rama.

The technical term for this is accretion, and it is what happens to a popular text over centuries: the front of a poem is a good place to store things. None of this makes the Bala Kanda less valuable. It makes it a different kind of object from the Ayodhya Kanda — an anthology attached to a tragedy.

sections.label: Book Two · Ayodhyā Kāṇḍa
sections.title: The Book of Ayodhya
sections.subtitle: Two promises, a hunchbacked servant, and the finest sustained piece of writing in the poem

blocks.html: If someone tells you the Ramayana is a story about a war with a demon king, hand them Book Two. There are no demons in it. There is no magic to speak of. Nobody is rescued. It is one hundred and nineteen chapters about a family destroying itself over a succession, and it contains almost everything the epic knows about grief, obligation, and the particular cruelty of people who are behaving correctly.
The Announcement

Dasharatha, old and increasingly afraid, calls his council and proposes to consecrate Rama as yuvarāja, prince regent, immediately. The assembly agrees with enthusiasm — the poem gives us the city's joy at some length, which is a deliberate setting of the height from which everything is about to fall. Preparations begin. Rama is told; he goes to his mother Kausalya, who begins a fast; he goes to Sita; the streets are hung with flags.

Bharata, significantly, is not in the city. He is away visiting his mother's family, and nobody sends for him. The poem does not editorialise about this. It simply arranges for Kaikeyi to be told, by someone who hates the arrangement, that her son has been got out of the way.
Manthara
Manthara is a hunchbacked servant who came with Kaikeyi from her father's house. She climbs to a terrace, sees the decorated city, learns what is happening, and goes to her mistress.

Here is the detail that matters most, and it is the one nearly every retelling drops. Kaikeyi's first reaction is delight. She is so pleased at the news that Rama is to be consecrated that she takes off a piece of jewellery and gives it to Manthara as a reward for bringing it. She loves Rama; the text has already established that Rama is closer to her than to his own mother. Everything that follows has to be built on top of that.

Manthara builds it in one conversation. Her argument is not moral, it is actuarial. When Rama is king, Bharata will at best be a subordinate and at worst be killed, because that is what happens to the brothers of new kings. Kausalya will be the queen mother and you will be her servant. Your son is away and unwarned; the timing is not an accident. Do you understand what has been done to you?

It takes a while. Kaikeyi resists, argues, defends Rama. Then something turns over in her, and when it turns it turns completely. She goes to the "chamber of anger," strips off her ornaments, and lies on the bare floor.
The Two Boons

Dasharatha comes to her that night in high spirits and finds her on the ground. And she reminds him of something he has forgotten: long ago, in a war between the gods and the asuras, he was wounded and unconscious, and Kaikeyi drove his chariot out of the battle and saved his life. He offered her two boons. She took none at the time and kept them.
She names them now. First: consecrate Bharata in Rama's place. Second: send Rama into the Dandaka forest for fourteen years, dressed in bark and deerskin, living as an ascetic.

Dasharatha's collapse is the most sustained piece of psychological writing in the epic. He does not agree and he does not refuse. He faints; he weeps; he begs; he offers her the kingdom itself; he tries to reason; he threatens; he pleads with her to take anything else; he tells her he will die of it; he calls her names no king should use. And through all of it he never once says the only sentence that would end the matter, which is no. He cannot. He has given his word, and in this poem a given word is load-bearing. Kaikeyi simply waits.
Rama's Answer
Rama is sent for. His father cannot speak, so Kaikeyi tells him herself, briskly, and adds that the king is too ashamed to say it aloud.

And Rama agrees at once. Not after a struggle — at once, and with something that reads almost like relief. He says he would go if his father merely wished it and would not need a reason. He asks that Bharata be looked after. He is more concerned with getting his father out of the position of having broken a promise than with anything happening to himself.

This composure is not presented as easy or as obviously admirable. It horrifies everyone around him. Lakshmana wants to kill the king and take the throne by force; Kausalya asks whether a son's duty to a father outranks his duty to a mother, which is a serious question and the text lets her ask it properly. Rama's answer is the same each time and it is not an argument so much as a position: his father's word must stand, and a man who abandons dharma to keep a kingdom has not kept anything.
Sita Insists

Rama goes to tell Sita, and tries to leave her behind. The exchange that follows is the most important thing in Book Two for anyone who wants to know who Sita is in the oldest telling, because the tradition's later image of her as an emblem of silent submission is not what is on the page.

She argues. She argues well. She quotes the principle that a wife shares her husband's fate. She points out that she was raised on these teachings and knows them at least as well as he does. She says the forest holds no terror for her that his absence does not exceed. And when he keeps refusing, she loses her temper and insults him: she says her father Janaka, king of Mithila, was badly deceived — he seems to have got, in the form of a man, a woman.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · Sita to Rama, on the Road Ahead (half-verse)
blocks.mn: "I will walk in front of you, crushing the kusha-grass and the thorns underfoot."

blocks.html: She wins the argument. Lakshmana wins his separately, by refusing to be left. Urmila, Lakshmana's wife of a few weeks, is not consulted and stays behind for fourteen years; Valmiki gives her almost nothing, and later poets — particularly in the Hindi and Maithili traditions — have gone back to fill that silence, sometimes at great length.
The City Follows

The three of them leave in bark cloth, and the population of Ayodhya walks out of the gates behind them. This is not metaphor; the poem means the citizens physically follow the chariot, weeping, refusing to turn back, saying that a city is where its prince is and the buildings can stay behind if they like. Rama has to escape them by having the charioteer drive on through the night while they sleep.

They reach the Ganga, where the poem introduces Guha, chief of the Nishadas — the same community as the hunter of the opening scene, a forest people outside the settled caste order. Rama embraces him as a friend and calls him brother; Guha and his men ferry them across and Guha grieves at the parting. It is a warm and completely unembarrassed passage, and you should hold on to it, because in Book Seven this same poem will do something extremely different with the question of who may do what.
Then Bharadvaja's hermitage at the confluence, and then Chitrakuta, where they build a hut of leaves and the exile settles into something almost like happiness.
How Dasharatha Dies
Back in Ayodhya, Dasharatha is dying of grief, and on the last night he tells Kausalya a story he has never told anyone.

blocks.tag: Story · The Sound at the Water

blocks.html: When he was young he had a skill he was proud of: śabdavedhī, the ability to shoot at a sound in the dark without seeing the target. One night in the rainy season he was by the river Sarayu waiting for game to come and drink. He heard the sound of a pot filling under water — exactly the sound an elephant makes drawing water in its trunk. He shot.

What cried out was a boy. Dasharatha ran to the bank and found an ascetic's son lying in the water with an arrow in him, who asked, before he died, only one thing: that the king go and tell his parents, who were blind, and who were waiting for the water.

He went. He carried the water to them. He told them what he had done. The old man cursed him — that he too would die grieving for a son — and then the two of them lay down beside their child's body and died.

"That curse has found me," Dasharatha tells Kausalya. And then, in the dark, calling out to a son who is three days' journey away in a forest, he dies. Valmiki does not give the boy a name; the name Śravaṇa Kumāra, by which every Indian child knows him, comes from later tradition.

Notice what that story does structurally. It takes a king who has just been destroyed by keeping a promise and reveals that he was, long ago, a man who killed an innocent from cover, by mistake, and was cursed for it. The epic is quietly insisting that nobody in it arrives clean.
Bharata Refuses

Bharata is fetched home, is told nothing on the road, and arrives to find his father dead and his brother gone and himself the beneficiary. His reaction is one of the most emphatic things in the poem: he denounces his mother in language of real violence, tells her she has murdered his father, disowns her, and refuses the throne absolutely.

Then he does the funeral rites and marches to Chitrakuta with the army, the ministers, the queens and a large part of the population, to bring Rama back. What follows is the longest ethical debate in the epic, conducted between two men each of whom is trying to give the kingdom to the other.

blocks.tag: Scriptural Lens · Jabali's Argument

blocks.html: In the middle of that debate the brahmin Jābāli speaks, and what he says is so unexpected that many readers assume it must be a corruption. It is not; it is in the text, and it is put in strong terms.

Jabali tells Rama, roughly: you are being sentimental about nothing. A man comes into the world alone and leaves it alone. Your attachment to a father who is dead is a category error — there is no one there to be loyal to. The rites for the dead are a clever invention; look at the offerings, which are simply food destroyed for nothing. Take the kingdom; there is no other world, and nothing beyond what can be seen.

Rama's reply is furious. He calls the argument the doctrine of a nāstika, one who denies, and says that a king who reasoned this way would be a thief with the manners of a Buddhist. Jabali then retreats, saying he argued that way only to persuade Rama to return and does not himself hold the view. Whether that retraction is original or a nervous later patch is a question scholars have raised, since it is exactly the sort of thing an anxious editor adds.

Either way, the passage is remarkable evidence: a full-blooded materialist position, stated clearly enough to be understood, preserved inside the most orthodox of Sanskrit narratives. The tradition did not hide the arguments against it. It answered them, sometimes badly, in public.

Rama will not come back. The exile was ordered by his father and will be completed. Finally Bharata takes Rama's sandals, puts them on his head, carries them to Ayodhya, sets them on the throne, and rules for fourteen years from a village outside the city — living himself as an ascetic in bark cloth, doing the work of government in the name of a pair of shoes.

That image is the answer Book Two gives to the question Book One asked. Is there a man of perfect conduct? Perhaps; but here are four or five people all trying to behave perfectly at the same time, and the result is a dead king, a broken family, an empty throne and a woman that history has never forgiven. Dharma in this book is not a rule you follow to a good outcome. It is a set of obligations that can point in different directions at once, and the poem knows it.

blocks.tag: Reflect · On Kaikeyi

blocks.html: Before you move on, spend a minute with Kaikeyi, who is the most hated woman in Indian literature and the only person in Book Two who acts decisively.

The text gives her a real case and then buries it: she is a junior queen with a son who will be nothing; the succession has been arranged while that son is out of town; she was promised two boons by a man who thought she would never use them. Manthara's analysis of the situation is, on the poem's own evidence, largely correct. And Kaikeyi is destroyed by having been right about the politics and wrong about everything else.

Several modern retellings — in Hindi, Kannada, Bengali and English — have gone back into her, and the results are worth reading. You do not have to like her. But if you find you cannot even hold her in view as a person, notice that, because it is the exact mechanism by which a tradition turns a character into a lesson.

sections.label: Book Three · Araṇya Kāṇḍa
sections.title: The Book of the Forest
sections.subtitle: A warning about weapons, a woman's severed nose, and the hinge of the entire epic

blocks.html: The forest in this poem is not scenery. It is a different legal order. In Ayodhya, actions are governed by promises, councils and inheritance; in the Dandaka, they are governed by whoever is strongest and hungriest. Rama walks out of one system into the other wearing bark cloth and carrying a bow, and Book Three is about what those two facts do to each other.

Ten of the fourteen years pass in a few chapters. They move between hermitages; they kill a rakshasa called Viradha; they visit Sharabhanga, who enters the fire; they visit Sutikshna; they spend a long time with Agastya, the sage who is remembered across south India as the one who came south and civilised it, and who gives Rama a bow of Vishnu's, two inexhaustible quivers and a sword.
The Sages' Request, and Sita's Objection

Early in the book, the ascetics of the forest come to Rama and show him what has been happening to them: heaps of bones, the remains of hermits eaten by rakshasas. They ask for protection. Rama gives his word that he will rid the forest of them.
And Sita takes him aside and tells him he is making a mistake. This chapter is not much quoted and it should be.

blocks.tag: Scriptural Lens · Sita on the Danger of Carrying Weapons

blocks.html: Sita begins by saying that there are three faults born of desire, and that the third is the subtle one. The first is lying. The second is going to another man's wife. The third is violence without enmity — harming beings who have done you no harm.

Then she tells him a story. There was once an ascetic in a forest, of perfect self-control. Indra, made uneasy by his austerity, came to him disguised as a soldier and left a sword with him for safekeeping. The ascetic, now responsible for a weapon, carried it everywhere so as not to lose it. And having a sword always to hand, he began, gradually, to change: the habit of the weapon worked backwards into the mind that held it, and in time he lost his gentleness altogether and fell.

Her argument is precise. You have taken up the life of an ascetic in the forest, she says, and you are proposing to kill rakshasas who have not harmed you, on behalf of others, in a place where you came to live quietly. Weapons and forests are a bad combination. I am not instructing you — I would not presume — but think about it.

Rama's reply is that he has given his word to men who were afraid, and that he would rather give up Lakshmana, or Sita, or his own life, than break a promise made to brahmins. She does not press it. The forest is subsequently full of killing, and the woman who warned against it is the person the killing eventually costs him. Whether Valmiki intended the irony or merely permitted it, it is one of the sharpest things in the epic — and it is spoken by the character the tradition later flattened into an emblem of obedience.
Panchavati and Shurpanakha

On Agastya's advice they settle at Panchavati on the Godavari, and there they are seen by Shurpanakha, Ravana's sister. She wants Rama. She says so directly — she is a rakshasi and does not do the things a woman in Ayodhya would do — and tells him she can go where she likes and that his human wife is thin and unsuitable and that she will eat her.

What follows is one of the passages that most reliably ambushes a modern reader. Rama does not simply refuse. He teases. He tells her that he already has a wife and that she should apply to his brother, who is unattached and would be lucky to have her. Lakshmana, taking up the joke, says he is only a servant and she would not want to be a servant's wife; better go back to Rama. She goes back and forth between them, being played with, and finally, in a rage, rushes at Sita — and Lakshmana takes his sword and cuts off her nose and her ears.

Read the passage in the Sanskrit and its register is broad, almost comic, until the instant it is not. She runs howling to her brother Khara; fourteen thousand rakshasas are sent; Rama fights them alone and kills all of them, along with Khara, Dushana and Trishira. Then she goes to Lanka, to Ravana, and describes Sita to him.

Later traditions were uneasy here and adjusted. Kamban's Tamil telling handles Shurpanakha with far more inwardness, giving her real desire and real humiliation; several folk and modern versions make her the wronged party outright, and some feminist retellings treat the mutilation as the epic's original sin — the injury that the whole war is a punishment for. All of that is commentary on a passage that Valmiki wrote as a joke that turns into a butchery. It is worth being honest that the joke is there.
Maricha and the Golden Deer

Ravana flies to the rakshasa Maricha — the same one Rama drove into the sea years earlier during Vishvamitra's sacrifice — and orders him to take the form of a golden deer and lure Rama away. Maricha refuses. Twice. And his refusal contains the epic's most quoted single line about Rama, spoken not by a devotee but by an enemy who has met him and is terrified:

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · Maricha Warns Ravana
blocks.sk:
रामो विग्रहवान्धर्मः साधुः सत्यपराक्रमः ।
राजा सर्वस्य लोकस्य देवानामिव वासवः ॥
blocks.tr:
rāmo vigrahavān dharmaḥ sādhuḥ satyaparākramaḥ |
rājā sarvasya lokasya devānām iva vāsavaḥ ||
blocks.mn: "Rama is dharma with a body on it — a good man, whose strength is his truth; the king of the whole world, as Indra is of the gods."

blocks.html: Ravana's answer is that Maricha may choose which of the two of them kills him. Maricha chooses Rama — better, he says, to die by an arrow than by this king's displeasure — and goes, knowing exactly what will happen, which makes him one of the few characters in the epic who acts with full knowledge of the outcome.

The deer appears at the hut, jewelled and impossible. Sita wants it. Rama, against Lakshmana's warning, follows it a long way and shoots it, and as it dies Maricha resumes his shape and calls out, in Rama's exact voice, Hā Sītā! Hā Lakṣmaṇa!

And here the poem does something that hurts. Sita hears the cry and orders Lakshmana to go. He refuses; he says no rakshasa can harm Rama and that he was told to stay. And Sita, frightened out of all judgement, says the worst thing available to her: she accuses him of wanting her, of having come to the forest for that reason, of waiting for his brother to die. He goes — shaking, saluting her — and she is alone.

The line drawn on the ground, which Sita crosses and must not cross, is not in Valmiki. There is no Lakṣmaṇa-rekhā in the Sanskrit text. It enters through later retellings and folk performance, where it has become so universal that the phrase is now ordinary Hindi for a boundary one must not overstep. It is a magnificent invention. It is not Valmiki's.
The Abduction

Ravana comes to the hut as a wandering mendicant in ochre, with a staff and a begging bowl, and Sita, alone and bound by the obligation to feed a guest, receives him. He praises her, tells her who he is, and asks her to be his queen. She refuses with contempt and warns him. He takes his own shape, seizes her, and carries her into the sky in his chariot.

The old vulture Jatayu, a friend of Dasharatha's, wakes and attacks him. He is enormous and he is very old, and the fight is described with great tenderness: he breaks the chariot, kills the mules, tears at Ravana with beak and talons — and Ravana cuts off his wings and leaves him dying. As they rise, Sita drops her ornaments in a bundle onto a hilltop where five monkeys are sitting and watching.

Rama comes back to an empty hut. What follows is several chapters of a man losing his mind: he questions the trees, the river, a deer, asking them where she is; he threatens the world; Lakshmana talks him down. Then they find Jatayu, who tells them the name Ravana and the direction south, and dies — and Rama performs the funeral rites for a bird with his own hands, and says that Jatayu has done for him what his own father could not.

The book ends with two more encounters as they move south: Kabandha, a headless monster whose cremation releases a gandharva who tells them to seek an alliance with the exiled monkey king Sugriva; and the ascetic Shabari, a woman of a forest tribe, who has waited her whole life to receive Rama, feeds him, and then enters the fire. (The detail everyone remembers — that she tasted each berry first to be sure it was sweet — is not in Valmiki. It comes from the later devotional tradition, where it carries an argument about whose love outranks whose ritual purity.)

blocks.tag: Reflect · The Hinge

blocks.html: Everything before this book is a family story; everything after it is a war story. And the pivot is not a battle or a curse. It is a sequence of ordinary bad decisions: a joke made at a woman's expense, a mutilation, a request for a pretty animal, a warning ignored, an accusation shouted in fear.

No god intervenes to cause the abduction. Every step of it is done by people, in character, for reasons you can follow. That is worth noticing in a text the tradition reads as the descent of Vishnu: at the exact moment when divine machinery would be most useful to the plot, Valmiki uses human error instead.

sections.label: Book Four · Kiṣkindhā Kāṇḍa
sections.title: The Book of Kishkindha
sections.subtitle: An alliance, a killing from behind a tree, and a monsoon that will not end

blocks.html: Book Four is the political book. It is about exiles making a deal, and about what each side has to do to keep it. It contains the epic's most beautiful writing about weather and its single most troubling act, and it ends with a hundred thousand monkeys walking off in four directions to look for one woman.
Hanuman's Sanskrit

On the hill Rishyamukha, the exiled monkey king Sugriva sees two armed men approaching and assumes his brother has sent assassins. He sends his minister to find out who they are, and the minister comes down the hill in the form of a wandering mendicant and addresses them.

This is our introduction to Hanuman, and it is not what one expects of a monkey god. He is introduced as a diplomat, and specifically as a speaker. When he has finished, Rama turns to Lakshmana and delivers a small lecture on the quality of his prose:

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · Rama on Hanuman's Speech
blocks.mn: "No one untrained in the Rigveda, who does not carry the Yajurveda, who is not learned in the Samaveda, could possibly speak like this."

blocks.html: Rama goes on: the man has spoken at length without a single fault of grammar, without hurry, without a wrong accent, using the middle register of the voice, and his face gave nothing away. A king with a minister like that, he says, will get everything he wants.

Keep this in view. The Hanuman of popular devotion is strength and unreasoning love. The Hanuman of Valmiki's introduction is a grammarian. Both are in the text, and the second one is the reason the fifth book works.
The Quarrel of the Brothers
The alliance is made at a fire: Rama will kill Vali and restore Sugriva to the throne of Kishkindha; Sugriva will find Sita. Then Sugriva explains how he lost the kingdom.

An asura called Mayavi challenged Vali at night. Vali chased him into a cave and told Sugriva to wait outside. Sugriva waited a year. Then blood came out of the cave, and the sounds of demons rejoicing, and he concluded his brother was dead. He blocked the mouth of the cave with a boulder so the asura could not follow, went home, and — pressed by the ministers, who would not leave the throne empty — was made king. Vali came back. He did not believe a word of it, drove Sugriva out with such fury that he had to flee to the one hill Vali could not enter because of a curse, and took Sugriva's wife Ruma into his own household.
That is the case, as told by the plaintiff. The poem lets us hear it only from Sugriva.
The Arrow from Behind the Tree

Rama first demonstrates his power — kicking the dried skeleton of the buffalo-demon Dundubhi a great distance, and driving one arrow through seven sāla trees in a line — and then sends Sugriva to challenge his brother.

The first duel fails: the brothers are so alike that Rama, watching from cover, cannot tell them apart and does not shoot, and Sugriva is nearly killed. For the second attempt Lakshmana hangs a garland of flowers round Sugriva's neck so he can be identified. Vali's wife Tara — the most politically intelligent character in this book — tries to stop her husband going out, on the grounds that a defeated challenger who returns immediately must have acquired an ally, and that the ally is reported to be Rama. Vali does not listen, because he cannot believe that a man famous for righteousness would take a side in someone else's family dispute.
The brothers fight. Rama draws from behind a tree and shoots Vali in the chest.

And Vali, dying, delivers an accusation that the poem does not soften, cut, or hurry past — and Rama gives an answer that has been argued about for two thousand years. That exchange is important enough that this course gives it a chapter of its own; we will take it apart in Part Three. For now, only this: the objection is in the text. Valmiki wrote it. Nobody had to invent a criticism of Rama here — the epic supplies it, in the mouth of the man on the ground with the arrow in him.
Tara

Tara's lament over Vali's body is one of the great grief-speeches in Sanskrit, and she is not finished. She holds the situation together: her son Angada is made heir; she becomes, in effect, part of the new administration; and later, when Lakshmana comes to Kishkindha in a killing rage, it is Tara who walks out to meet him — reportedly having been drinking, which the poem mentions without embarrassment — and talks him down.

That episode is worth its own sentence. The rains have come, Sugriva has been installed, and Sugriva has done nothing at all about Sita for four months: he is in the palace, with wives, drinking. Rama, waiting on the mountain Prasravana, sends Lakshmana to remind him. Lakshmana arrives ready to burn the city down. Tara meets him at the gate, tells him the truth (the army has in fact been summoned and is arriving), points out that a man who has just spent years in exile might be forgiven a few weeks of enjoying his kingdom, and defuses him. Sugriva then does everything he promised.
The Rains

The monsoon chapters in this book are the reason poets love the Kishkindha Kanda. Rama sits in a cave on a wet mountain for four months with nothing to do, and the poem gives us the season in enormous detail — the clouds like elephants, the frogs starting up, the rivers filling, the peacocks, the roads impassable, the whole world coupling and green — and against it, one man who cannot move, cannot fight, cannot search, and does not know whether his wife is alive.

It is the oldest trick in Indian poetry, the season against the mood, and here it is being done at close to full strength. Rama in the rain is the most human he is anywhere in the epic. He weeps; he says he will not survive; Lakshmana, who is by now practised at this, keeps him going.
The Search, and the Shore

When the rains end, the vanara armies are summoned and sent to the four quarters of the world. The poem's geography here is a wonderful document in itself — a long list of peoples, mountains and rivers that reads like a mental map of the known world, and which includes, in the northern and western directions, names that historians take seriously as evidence for when these chapters were written.

The southern party — Angada, Jambavan the bear, Hanuman — is the one that matters. They exhaust their time limit, get lost in an underground cavern, emerge on the wrong shore, and decide to fast to death rather than return failures. While they are sitting there discussing whose fault it is, they mention Jatayu's name, and out of a cave comes his brother Sampati, wingless and ancient, who flew too near the sun in his youth. He tells them that with the sight of his kind he can see, a hundred leagues off across the water, a woman in a grove in Lanka.

So they go to the edge of the sea. And nobody can cross it. Each of them calculates aloud what distance he can jump; Angada can go and not return. And Jambavan turns to Hanuman, who has been sitting apart saying nothing, and begins to tell him who he is.

blocks.tag: Symbolic Lens · Being Told What You Are

blocks.html: Hanuman does not know his own strength — not as modesty, but literally. As a child he flew at the sun believing it was fruit, was struck down by Indra, and was afterwards cursed by the sages he had troubled to forget his powers until someone reminded him of them.

So the last chapter of Book Four is a passage in which an old bear stands on a beach and recites to a monkey the facts of his own birth, his father the wind, what he did as an infant, and what he is capable of. And as he listens, Hanuman begins to grow.

Whatever else one thinks about this epic, that is an extraordinary piece of psychology to find at the end of a political book from the middle of the first millennium BCE. The tradition's reading has been unanimous and, for once, hard to improve on: the obstacle was never the ocean.

sections.label: Book Five · Sundara Kāṇḍa
sections.title: The Beautiful Book
sections.subtitle: One monkey, one ocean, one night in a hostile city — and the only book of the seven in which nothing is lost

blocks.html: Across south India there are households where the Sundara Kanda is read aloud from beginning to end when someone is ill, when a case is going badly, when a child is sitting an examination, when a family is waiting for news. Not the Ramayana — this book of it. Sixty-eight chapters, often read over a week, or over forty days, or in a single unbroken night. No other section of any Indian epic has this independent devotional life, and there is a reason for it, which we will get to at the end.
It opens with Hanuman standing on a mountain by the sea, and with one of the most quietly perfect first lines in Sanskrit.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · The First Verse of the Sundara Kāṇḍa
blocks.sk:
ततो रावणनीतायाः सीतायाः शत्रुकर्शनः ।
इयेष पदमन्वेष्टुं चारणाचरिते पथि ॥
blocks.tr:
tato rāvaṇanītāyāḥ sītāyāḥ śatrukarśanaḥ |
iyeṣa padam anveṣṭuṁ cāraṇācarite pathi ||
blocks.mn: "Then, to find the trace of Sita, who had been carried off by Ravana, the crusher of enemies resolved upon the road that the sky-travellers travel."

blocks.html: Padam anveṣṭum — to search for a footprint, a trace, a place. And the road he takes to look for a footprint is the one with no ground under it.
The Leap

The take-off is described physically and at length, because Valmiki wants you to feel the mass of the thing. Hanuman swells; he presses down on Mount Mahendra until water spurts from its sides and animals bolt from their caves and trees shed their flowers; the whole mountain sinks under his crouch. Then he goes, and the recoil throws the trees on the summit up into the air behind him so that for a moment they fly alongside, carrying their blossoms out over the water before dropping — an image nobody who reads it forgets.
Three things happen to him in the air, and it is worth seeing that he passes each in a different way.

items: Mainaka, a golden mountain, rises out of the sea to offer him a place to rest — repaying an ancient debt to Hanuman's father, the wind, who once saved him from Indra. Hanuman touches the peak with his hand as a courtesy and declines: he has undertaken a task and will not stop until it is done. He passes by refusing help.

Surasa, mother of the serpents, is sent by the gods to test him. She says she has a boon that everything passing this way must go through her mouth. Hanuman offers to enter it. She opens her mouth wide; he grows; she grows wider; he grows again — and then, abruptly, he shrinks to the size of a thumb, darts in and out, and stands beside her having satisfied the letter of the boon exactly. He passes by wit.

Simhika catches him from below by seizing his shadow on the water and dragging him down. He allows himself to be pulled toward her, then makes himself enormous, and when she opens her mouth he dives into it and tears her apart from inside. He passes by force.

blocks.html: The Sundara Kanda is the book people memorise, and this triad is one reason. It teaches, in about a hundred verses, the three things a messenger needs: the discipline to refuse a comfortable delay, the flexibility to satisfy an obstacle rather than fight it, and the willingness to destroy something when destruction is the only thing left.
The City

He lands on a hill above Lanka at evening, and the poem stops dead to describe the city — and it is important to see how the description is written. Valmiki is not describing the fortress of an enemy. He is dazzled. Ramparts of gold; seven-storeyed mansions; gateways with machines on them; crystal floors; women's voices and the sound of instruments coming up in the dusk; parks, tanks, flowering trees. Hanuman looks at it and thinks that it is beautiful, and then thinks that taking it will be extremely difficult.

He shrinks himself to the size of a cat and goes in over the wall at night. The guardian goddess of the city, Lankini, strikes him; he hits her back with his left hand, holding back because she is female; and she tells him that it was long ago prophesied that when a monkey overcame her, the end of the rakshasas had begun.
The Night Search
What follows is one of the strangest sequences in the epic: many chapters of a small monkey moving through the private apartments of a sleeping city, looking at women.

He searches house by house, and then Ravana's palace, and then the inner apartments, where hundreds of women lie asleep after a night of music and drinking, in every posture, and where the poem lingers with frank and enormous relish. He finds Mandodari, Ravana's chief queen, and for a moment believes he has found Sita, and rejoices, and then reasons his way out of it: Sita would not be sleeping ornamented in a rakshasa's bed.

Then he stops and reproaches himself. He has been looking at other men's wives asleep — which is precisely a thing that a person of his discipline must not do. And the resolution he reaches is worth reading closely, because it is a piece of moral reasoning of a kind we do not usually credit to this literature.

blocks.tag: Scriptural Lens · Hanuman Examines His Own Mind

blocks.html: His argument has two parts. The first is practical: a woman who is lost must be looked for among women, and there is nowhere else to search. You do not find a missing thing by refusing to look in the place it would be.

The second is the interesting one. He says that the fault of looking lies not in the eye but in the mind, and he examines his own — and finds that it has not moved. He looked at all these women and felt nothing but the wish to find one particular person. The organ acted; the mind stayed where it was; therefore no transgression has occurred.

You may or may not accept the reasoning. What matters is the form of it: this is an ethics of interior state rather than of external act, argued by a character in the middle of an adventure story, and it is one of the reasons Hanuman became, for so much of India, the model of what discipline actually looks like — not a man who avoids the world, but one who has checked.

He does not find her. He searches everything, twice, and then sits down in real despair and thinks about what happens if he goes back with nothing: Rama will die, and then Lakshmana, and then Bharata, and Shatrughna, and Kausalya — he follows the whole chain of consequences down. He decides he will not return without news. And then he sees, over a wall he has not crossed, a grove of ashoka trees.
Under the Shinshapa Tree

He climbs into a śiṁśapā tree and looks down, and there she is, and Valmiki's description is a series of similes for something obscured: a flame wrapped in smoke, a stream choked with weeds, a memory that is fading, a star fallen to earth, a doe among hounds. She is filthy, in a single soiled garment, thin from fasting, sitting on the ground, surrounded by rakshasa women who have been set to break her.

And Hanuman has to watch, from the tree, without being able to act, through a night that includes: Ravana arriving to press his case with a mixture of flattery, argument and open threat; Sita answering him with a blade of grass held between them, refusing to speak to him directly; Ravana giving her two months and promising that after that his cooks will prepare her for his breakfast; the rakshasis crowding round afterwards to work on her with threats of being eaten; and then Sita, at the end of her strength, deciding to hang herself from a branch with her own braid of hair.

One thing lightens it. A rakshasi called Trijata wakes and tells the others to stop, because she has had a dream: Rama on a white elephant, and Ravana shaved bald, dressed in red, smeared with oil, drunk, falling from a chariot and being dragged south on a donkey. The others are frightened enough to back off. It is the only kindness Sita receives in captivity, and it comes from one of her jailers.
What Language to Use
Now Hanuman has his problem, and it is a problem of speech, which is fitting for a character introduced as a speaker.

He must make contact without terrifying her. If he drops out of the tree she will scream and the guards will come. If he speaks Sanskrit in the manner of a learned brahmin, he reasons, she will assume he is Ravana in another disguise, since that is exactly the form Ravana took at the hut. So he decides to use what the text calls mānuṣam vākyam — ordinary human speech, the plain register.

And he begins, quietly, from up in the branches, not addressing her at all, to tell a story: there was a king of the Ikshvakus called Dasharatha, and he had a son. He tells the whole thing from the beginning, at low volume, in simple words, until the woman on the ground below has heard her own life told back to her by an invisible voice and looks up.
It is, I think, the best-constructed scene in the poem. Everything Hanuman was introduced as — the diplomat, the grammarian, the reader of situations — is used here, and none of it is strength.

She still does not believe him; she suspects Ravana. He gives her Rama's signet ring. And she takes it and turns it over and it is his, and the poem says she wept and it was as though her husband had come.
The Offer She Refuses
Hanuman offers to carry her out on his back, right now, over the ocean. It is a serious offer and he can do it.

Sita refuses, and gives reasons, and the reasons are hers. First, practically, she doubts his ability to carry her — which he answers by growing to a great size until she is convinced. Then, the two real ones. She will not willingly touch the body of another man; Ravana carried her, but she was seized, and that is a different thing, and she will not now do voluntarily what was done to her by force. And second — this one is political — Rama's honour requires that he come himself. If she is smuggled out by a servant, the world will say the descendant of Raghu could not recover his own wife. She will not steal her own rescue from him.

She gives Hanuman her cūḍāmaṇi, the jewel from her hair, and a private token that no one else could know: the day at Chitrakuta when a crow — Indra's son in that form — attacked her and drew blood, and Rama, having no proper weapon to hand, took a blade of grass, charged it with the brahmastra, and put out one of the bird's eyes. Tell him that, she says. And tell him he has one month.
The Fire
And then Hanuman decides, on his own initiative, that reconnaissance is not enough — that he should test the enemy's strength while he is here. So he tears the ashoka grove to pieces.

The rakshasa guards come and die. Then champions; then Jambumali; then seven ministers' sons; then Aksha, Ravana's own son.
