Finally Indrajit, Ravana's eldest, binds him with the brahmāstra — and Hanuman, who knows the weapon must be honoured and also knows that being taken prisoner is the fastest way to get an audience with Ravana, lets it hold him even though he could shrug it off.
In the court, no seat is offered to him. So he coils his own tail into a tower and sits on top of it, higher than the throne. He announces himself:

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · Hanuman Names Himself
blocks.sk:
जयत्यतिबलो रामो लक्ष्मणश्च महाबलः ।
दासोऽहं कोसलेन्द्रस्य रामस्याक्लिष्टकर्मणः ॥
blocks.tr:
jayaty atibalo rāmo lakṣmaṇaś ca mahābalaḥ |
dāso 'haṁ kosalendrasya rāmasyākliṣṭakarmaṇaḥ ||
blocks.mn: "Victory to Rama of surpassing strength, and to mighty Lakshmana. I am the servant of the lord of Kosala, Rama, whose deeds cost him no effort."

blocks.html: Ravana orders him killed. Vibhishana, Ravana's youngest brother, objects on a point of law: an envoy may not be executed; mutilate him, disfigure him, beat him, but killing a messenger is not done. So Ravana has his tail wrapped in oiled cloth and set alight, and he is paraded through the streets.

Word reaches Sita, who prays to Agni to be cool to him. Hanuman notices that his tail is burning and that he cannot feel it. Then he shrinks, slips his bonds, grows again, and goes across the roofs of Lanka setting the city on fire — mansion by mansion, from the top, in the wind, with a torch attached to him.

And in the middle of it, in the air above a burning city, he is seized by the worst thought he has had: Sita is in there. He stands appalled at what he may have just done. Then he reasons it out — the fire did not burn him, so it will not have burned her — and the voices of the sky-beings confirm she is safe, and he goes back to the grove to see her one more time before he leaves.

He crosses the ocean the other way. On the far shore the search party hears him coming and knows, before he lands, from the noise he is making, that the news is good. He says two words that every reciter of this book waits for: dṛṣṭā sītā — "Sita has been seen." Then, because they are monkeys and have been under discipline for months, they detour to raid Sugriva's private honey-grove and get spectacularly drunk, and the guards' furious report of the vandalism is how Sugriva knows the mission succeeded.
Why This Book Stands Alone
Now the question we started with. Why is this the book that people recite by itself?

The plainest answer is structural. It is the only one of the seven in which nothing goes wrong. Book Two ends in exile, Three in abduction, Four in delay, Six in a public humiliation, Seven in a series of deaths. Book Five is a complete action, undertaken against impossible odds by someone who had to be persuaded he could do it at all, which succeeds. If you are reading aloud in a house where something is badly wrong, that is the shape you want in the room.

The devotional answer goes further: that the Sundara Kanda is the book of the intermediary. Rama is unreachable; Sita cannot get out; between them is a servant who crosses the impassable thing in both directions and makes the two ends of a broken relation aware of each other. Vaishnava theology has a technical vocabulary for that role, and Hanuman is its illustration. When people read this book over a sick relative, they are not asking for a monkey to appear. They are rehearsing the proposition that the gap can be crossed.

blocks.tag: Practice · How the Book Is Actually Read

blocks.html: If you want to do this, the ordinary forms are simple. Some read all sixty-eight sargas in a single sitting, which takes several hours. Some read it over nine days, or over forty. Some read only sarga 36 and 38 — the meeting with Sita — as a daily practice. In Telugu and Tamil households a parayana of the Sundara Kanda is a normal response to trouble in the way that a novena is elsewhere.

You do not need Sanskrit. Good translations exist in every Indian language and in English, and the tradition itself has never insisted that this particular book be kept in the original — which is itself telling, since it is the book that is most about making yourself understood.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · A Later Verse on Hanuman, Recited Everywhere
blocks.sk:
यत्र यत्र रघुनाथकीर्तनं तत्र तत्र कृतमस्तकाञ्जलिम् ।
बाष्पवारिपरिपूर्णलोचनं मारुतिं नमत राक्षसान्तकम् ॥
blocks.tr:
yatra yatra raghunāthakīrtanaṁ tatra tatra kṛtamastakāñjalim |
bāṣpavāriparipūrṇalocanaṁ mārutiṁ namata rākṣasāntakam ||
blocks.mn: "Wherever the Lord of the Raghus is sung of, there he stands with his palms joined at his forehead and his eyes brimming with tears — bow to the son of the Wind, the ender of the rakshasas."
blocks.src: — A traditional verse in praise of Hanuman, not from Vālmīki; of uncertain authorship and much later date

blocks.html: A last small note about the name. Nobody is certain why Book Five is called "the beautiful one." The traditional explanations are that Hanuman was called Sundara by his mother, or simply that everything in the book — the ocean, the flight, the city, Sita, the deed — is beautiful. Both are guesses offered by commentators long after the fact. The honest position is that the title is old, its reason is lost, and the book has spent two thousand years earning it retrospectively.

sections.label: Book Six · Yuddha Kāṇḍa
sections.title: The Book of War
sections.subtitle: A promise of refuge, a causeway, a very long battle, and a cold sentence at the end of it

blocks.html: The war book is the longest of the seven and, for long stretches, the least interesting to read — as war books generally are, everywhere, in every literature. It is formulaic by design: champions meet, boast, exchange arrows, one falls, the armies react, repeat. What makes it worth your attention are the four or five places where the formula stops.
Vibhishana Comes Over

In Lanka, Ravana's youngest brother tells him plainly to give Sita back — that the war is unwinnable, that the cause is wrong, and that keeping another man's wife by force is not a policy. Ravana insults him and, in some tellings, kicks him. Vibhishana leaves, with four companions, and flies across the water to hover above Rama's army and ask for asylum.

Rama's council splits. Sugriva's position is blunt: he is a rakshasa, he is the enemy's brother, kill him now. Others agree. Hanuman, characteristically, argues from the evidence of the man's speech and bearing rather than from category. And Rama then makes the statement that became, for one entire school of Indian theology, the centre of everything:

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · The Vow of Refuge
blocks.sk:
सकृदेव प्रपन्नाय तवास्मीति च याचते ।
अभयं सर्वभूतेभ्यो ददाम्येतद्व्रतं मम ॥
blocks.tr:
sakṛd eva prapannāya tavāsmīti ca yācate |
abhayaṁ sarvabhūtebhyo dadāmy etad vratam mama ||
blocks.mn: "To anyone who has come to me even once, and says 'I am yours,' and asks — I give safety from all beings. That is my vow."

blocks.html: In the Srivaishnava tradition of south India this verse, and the passage around it, is the scriptural anchor of śaraṇāgati — surrender — the doctrine that the one requirement is to turn up and say so, once, and that nothing else is being asked. Ramanuja's school built a great deal on this. It is also, read simply as narrative, a startling piece of politics: the commander of an army about to besiege a city accepts the defection of the enemy king's brother on the sole ground that he asked.
The Causeway

The army reaches the shore and cannot cross. Rama lies down on the sand facing the sea and fasts for three days, formally petitioning the ocean to give way. Nothing happens. So he loses his temper, takes up a weapon capable of drying the sea to its bed, and prepares to use it — at which point the ocean appears in person, apologetically, and explains that he cannot simply stop being deep, but that there is a man in the army who can solve the problem.

That is Nala, son of the divine architect Vishvakarma, and the vanaras build under his direction: five days' work, rocks and trees thrown into the water, the poem giving the causeway's dimensions in yojanas. The army crosses.

The squirrel is not in Valmiki. The much-loved story — a small squirrel carrying grains of sand to help, Rama stroking its back and leaving three white stripes — belongs to the later regional traditions, and is especially at home in Tamil and Telugu tellings. It is a beautiful piece of theology about the value of small offerings. It is not part of the Sanskrit text, and if you have been told it is, you have been told wrong by someone who loved it.
The Battle
Angada is sent as a last envoy and returns with nothing. Then the siege, and it goes on for many chapters. The moments that lift out of it:

items: The serpent-arrows. Indrajit binds Rama and Lakshmana in nāgapāśa, coils of living snakes, and both lie unconscious and apparently dead before the whole army. They are freed by the arrival of Garuda, the eagle who eats serpents, at whose approach the bonds simply let go.

Kumbhakarna. Ravana's gigantic brother, cursed to sleep for months at a stretch, is woken by an operation involving elephants walking on him. And when he is awake, the first thing he does is tell Ravana that the war is his own fault and that abducting Sita was wrong — and the second thing he does is go out and fight for him anyway, because he is his brother. He is killed with enormous difficulty, and the poem gives him real weight.

The mountain of herbs. Lakshmana is struck down by a weapon of Ravana's and is dying. The physician Sushena names four healing herbs that grow on a particular Himalayan mountain; Hanuman flies north, cannot identify the plants when he arrives, and so picks up the entire mountain and brings it back — an image so beloved that it is how Hanuman is most often depicted in sculpture across India.

Indrajit. Ravana's son is the most dangerous enemy in the book: he fights invisible, he uses illusion, and at one point he conjures a false Sita and beheads her in the air in front of the army to break their morale. He is finally killed by Lakshmana at Nikumbhila, where he had gone to complete a rite that would have made him unbeatable — interrupted, on Vibhishana's advice, before it was finished.

blocks.html: The Death of Ravana

The last duel takes days. Indra sends his own chariot and charioteer down for Rama, who has been fighting on foot against a flying opponent. Rama cuts off Ravana's heads and they grow back as fast as he can remove them. Finally Agastya teaches him a hymn to the sun — the Āditya-hṛdaya, still recited daily by many people, though its self-contained hymnic form and its abrupt arrival at this point in the narrative have long made readers suspect it of being an insertion — and then, with a weapon given by Agastya and charged by Brahma, Rama shoots Ravana through the chest and he falls.

What the poem does next is the reason Part Three of this course has a chapter on Ravana. It does not gloat. Vibhishana's grief is given at length. Mandodari's lament over her husband's body is a serious piece of poetry, and in it she says things about him — that he was learned, that he was a great king, that he had everything and lost it over one woman he could not have — that are treated as true. And when Vibhishana, angry, refuses to perform the funeral rites for a brother who behaved as Ravana did, Rama overrules him in one sentence that we will come back to.
And Then Rama Speaks to Sita
Sita is brought out of the grove, bathed, dressed, carried in a litter. The army wants to see her. Rama orders that she be brought on foot through the crowd.
And then, in front of everyone, he tells her that he did not do this for her.

This is the passage that has damaged the Ramayana for more readers than anything else in it, and it deserves to be handled at full length rather than in the last paragraph of a chapter about a war. It is the subject of the next section but one. For the moment, the outline: Rama's speech; Sita's reply, which is a rebuke and not a plea; the fire; Agni returning her; the gods' revelation of who Rama is; the reconciliation.

Then the flight home in Ravana's captured aerial chariot, the Puṣpaka, with Rama pointing out the landmarks of the whole campaign to Sita from the air on the way north — the bridge, the shore, Kishkindha, the forest, the hut. They stop for Bharadvaja; Hanuman is sent ahead to Nandigrama to warn Bharata, who has been living for fourteen years in bark cloth beside a pair of sandals and has publicly announced that if Rama is not back on the appointed day he will enter fire.

And then the consecration that Book Two began preparing and did not deliver. The reign that follows is described in the terms that gave Indian political language the phrase Rāma-rājya: no one grieving, no disease, no widows mourning, no fear of thieves or wild animals, the rains coming when needed, the old not burying the young.

The book ends with a phalaśruti — the traditional closing passage promising benefits to those who have heard the poem: long life, sons, the removal of sin, reunion for those who are separated. It is the way a finished Sanskrit work says goodbye.

blocks.tag: Historical Lens · The Poem Ends Here

blocks.html: Stop and register what has just happened, because it is the strongest single piece of evidence in the whole textual argument. The story is complete: the exile served, the wife recovered, the enemy killed, the brother restored, the kingdom taken up, the golden age begun. The narrator has told you what you will gain by having listened. This is a conclusion.

Everything in Book Seven happens after a text that has already finished. That does not make Book Seven false, or unimportant, or removable — it has been part of the Ramayana for the whole of its recorded manuscript history. But it does mean that when you turn the page, you are turning it into a different room, built later, onto a house that was already standing.

sections.label: Book Seven · Uttara Kāṇḍa
sections.title: The Last Book
sections.subtitle: Everything that happens after the happy ending — and it is not a coda, it is a second tragedy

blocks.html: Most people who love the Ramayana stop at the coronation. Most performances stop there; Dussehra and Diwali stop there; a great many published retellings stop there. And then there is a seventh book, which nearly everyone has heard of and comparatively few have read, in which the king who was just crowned banishes his pregnant wife on the strength of a rumour, kills an ascetic for practising austerities above his caste, loses his wife permanently, loses his brother, and walks into a river.

Whatever else you conclude about it, do not think of the Uttara Kanda as an appendix. It is the part of the tradition that takes the epic's own central claim — that here was a man of perfect conduct — and puts it under a load until something gives.
The First Half: Where Ravana Came From

The book opens with the sages coming to congratulate Rama, and Agastya staying behind to tell him who it was that he killed. Roughly the first third of the book is Ravana's biography, told in retrospect, and it is the main source for almost everything the tradition knows about him.

He is the grandson of Pulastya, one of Brahma's mind-born sons, and the son of the sage Vishrava by the rakshasa woman Kaikasi — half brahmin by descent, which the tradition never forgets. Kumbhakarna and Vibhishana are his brothers, Shurpanakha his sister, and Kubera the lord of wealth is his half-brother, from whom he takes Lanka and the flying chariot Pushpaka by force. He performs austerities for ten thousand years, cutting off his own heads one at a time and offering them into the fire, and receives the boon that undoes the world. He conquers in every direction; he defeats gods; he is at one point picked up by Vali and carried under his arm for a while, which the poem includes with evident amusement.
And there are two episodes in this biography that the reader of the earlier books needs, because they are the text's answer to a question the earlier books do not answer.

blocks.tag: Scriptural Lens · Why Ravana Never Touched Sita

blocks.html: In Book Five, Ravana threatens, flatters and terrifies Sita — and does not touch her. Readers have asked for centuries why a rakshasa king who has conquered the three worlds does not simply do what he likes. Book Seven answers with a curse.

Ravana had once seized the apsaras Rambha, who told him she was pledged to Nalakubara, Kubera's son, and therefore his own daughter-in-law by relation. He forced her regardless. Nalakubara, hearing of it, pronounced a curse of the specific and mechanical kind this literature specialises in: if Ravana ever again took a woman who was unwilling, his head would split into seven pieces.

So the restraint in the ashoka grove is not virtue. It is a technical limit, imposed by someone he had already injured, and it is the reason there is a two-month deadline and a campaign of psychological pressure instead of an assault. A second episode, in which Ravana assaults the ascetic Vedavatī and she enters fire swearing to be reborn as the cause of his destruction, is read in parts of the tradition as an account of Sita's real origin.

It is worth noticing what this back-story is for. It exists to secure Sita's chastity as a fact of plot rather than as her word for it. The text is anxious about exactly the thing that will destroy her in the second half of this same book — and it is anxious enough to go back and legislate it into the past.
The Rumour
Then the book turns. Sita is pregnant. Rama is happy; he asks her what she would like, and she says she would like to visit the hermitages by the Ganga again. He promises she will go tomorrow.

That evening he asks his informants what the city is saying about him. They do not want to answer. He insists. And they tell him: people are talking about Sita — that she lived a year in Ravana's house, that the king has taken her back, and that now, since the king does it, husbands in Ayodhya will have to put up with the same from their own wives. The poem gives the source: a washerman, quarrelling with his wife, throwing her out and saying that he is not Rama, to accept a woman who has lived in another man's house.

Rama summons his brothers. He tells them that ill fame is unbearable, that the good name of the Ikshvakus must be preserved, that he knows she is innocent — he says this explicitly; the text does not permit the reading that he had doubts — and that she must go. He orders Lakshmana to take her, on the pretext of the visit she asked for, across the Ganga, to leave her near Valmiki's hermitage, and to say nothing until it is done.
And he forbids anyone to argue with him. That is the sentence that closes the discussion: whoever speaks against this, I will treat as an enemy.

Lakshmana takes her across in a boat. She is cheerful; she has brought gifts for the sages' wives. On the far bank he breaks down and tells her. She faints. When she comes round, what she says is not a curse. She asks him to convey to the king that she knows he knows she is innocent; that she will not kill herself because she is carrying the line of the Ikshvakus; and — this is the part that is hardest to read — that he should go home and do his duty and be well.

Valmiki finds her weeping and takes her in. The twins are born in the hermitage. And the poet who opened this epic by cursing a hunter over a dead bird raises the abandoned wife of its hero, and teaches her sons to sing the poem.
Shambuka

In the middle of all this the book places an episode of a completely different kind, in which a brahmin's son dies before his time, Narada explains the cause, and Rama takes up a weapon and goes out to correct it. It is the passage that has made the Ramayana a battleground in modern Indian politics, and it gets its own chapter in Part Three. I am not going to summarise it here in a way that lets you pass over it.
The Horse Sacrifice

Years pass. Rama undertakes an aśvamedha, the imperial horse sacrifice, which requires the king's wife to be present. He does not remarry. He has a golden image of Sita made and placed beside him for the rite — and the tradition has always laid weight on this: that he ruled for decades and took no other queen, which was, for a king with that need for heirs, not a small thing.

Valmiki comes to the sacrifice with his two pupils, who sing the Ramayana to the assembly in twenty sessions. The court is transfixed. Rama listens to his own story, does not at first understand what he is hearing, and then looks at the two boys and sees his own face.

He sends word that if Sita is willing to swear her purity before the assembly, he will take her back. Valmiki brings her. He stands and testifies to her innocence himself, on the strength of his own accumulated austerity — an extraordinary intervention, the author of the poem stepping into it as a character to defend her.
And Sita comes forward, in ochre robes, eyes down, and speaks. And she does not swear the oath she was asked for. She swears a different one.

blocks.tag: Sanskrit · Sita's Last Words
blocks.sk:
यथाहं राघवादन्यं मनसापि न चिन्तये ।
तथा मे माधवी देवी विवरं दातुमर्हति ॥
blocks.tr:
yathāhaṁ rāghavād anyaṁ manasāpi na cintaye |
tathā me mādhavī devī vivaraṁ dātum arhati ||
blocks.mn: "As I have never thought of any man but Raghava, not even in my mind — so let the goddess Madhavi open and take me in."

blocks.html: The earth opens. A throne comes up out of it, carried by serpents, and on it the goddess Earth, who takes Sita in her arms, seats her beside her, and goes back down. Flowers fall. The assembly cries out. And the ground closes over the daughter who was found in a furrow.

Read the oath again and see what she has done with it. She was asked to prove herself in public a second time. She uses the form of the proof — the conditional oath, if I am telling the truth, then let this happen — and attaches to it, as the consequence, her own permanent departure. Her innocence and her disappearance are established by the same sentence. It is the last thing she says in the poem, and it is a refusal.
The River
Rama's reaction is fury: he threatens the Earth, demands her back, has to be calmed by Brahma, who tells him he will see her again but not here. He rules on, alone, for a very long time.
The ending, when it comes, is built out of the same machinery that has run the whole epic — a promise that cannot be broken, and a brother who takes the consequence.

An ascetic arrives asking for a private interview, on the condition that anyone who interrupts must be put to death. Rama agrees and posts Lakshmana at the door. The visitor is Time, come to tell him his work is finished. While they are speaking, the sage Durvasa arrives and demands to be admitted at once, threatening to curse the entire kingdom if he is kept waiting. Lakshmana stands there and does the arithmetic: the kingdom, or himself. He walks in.

Rama cannot execute his brother and cannot break his word. His advisers give him the formula: to abandon the virtuous is the equivalent of killing them. So he renounces Lakshmana, who goes to the Sarayu, sits down at the water's edge, stops his breath, and leaves his body.

Then Rama divides the kingdom between his sons, sets his affairs in order, and walks out of Ayodhya to the river in the early morning. And the city goes with him — the citizens, the ministers, the women, the children, the animals, Hanuman and Sugriva and the vanaras, the whole population of the place, walking behind him in silence down to the water. And they go into the Sarayu, all of them, and the poem ends.

blocks.tag: Reflect · The Two Endings

blocks.html: You now have two endings to the Ramayana, and they are irreconcilable, and both are in the manuscripts.
The first ends with a coronation, a golden age, and a promise that whoever hears this poem will be reunited with those they have been separated from. It is the ending that Diwali celebrates.

The second ends with a woman leaving through the floor, a brother dying at a riverbank because of a rule about doorways, and a king walking into water followed by everyone he ever ruled. It is the ending that the Uttara Kanda gives, and its mood — that the cost of a perfectly kept word is everything you have — is unmistakably the mood of the man who wrote the second book.

You do not have to choose. But you should know which one you are holding, and you should know that when someone tells you what the Ramayana teaches, the first thing to establish is where they stopped reading.
॥ श्री राम ॥

sections.label: Question 01 · The Fire
sections.title: Sita
sections.subtitle: The ordeal, the banishment, and what can honestly be said about the hardest passages in the poem

blocks.html: This is the chapter where a course like this one usually goes wrong, in one of two directions. It either explains the difficulty away — a chain of readings, each individually respectable, whose combined effect is that nothing troubling has occurred — or it uses the difficulty as a weapon, quoting the worst lines with obvious pleasure and drawing conclusions about a whole civilisation. I am going to try to do neither. First what the text says. Then how the tradition has read it. Then how it has been criticised. And then, at the end, one honest observation about the argument that is most often used to make the problem disappear.
What Rama Actually Says, in Book Six

The war is over. Ravana is dead. Sita has been brought from the grove, bathed and dressed, and Rama has insisted that she come to him on foot through the crowd, saying that a woman's veil is her conduct and that in a crisis she may be seen.

Then he speaks, and the temperature of the poem drops. He tells her, in front of the assembled armies, that he has done what a man must do: he has avenged the insult, wiped out the affront to his family, and recovered his honour. He tells her that this effort was not made for her sake. He says that suspicion attaches to a woman who has lived in another man's house, that Ravana looked at her and touched her, and that he cannot take her back — a man of his lineage cannot. And then he says the sentence that even the poem's most loyal readers find hard to get past: go wherever you wish; I have no further use for you. And he offers her a list of destinations: Lakshmana, or Bharata, or Shatrughna, or Sugriva, or Vibhishana — whichever she likes.
That list is not an accident of translation. It is in the Sanskrit, and it is the most brutal thing anyone says to anyone in the Ramayana.
What Sita Says Back
Her reply is not a plea. It is a rebuke, and it is delivered in public, and she has the better of the argument at every point.

She asks why he is speaking to her in the manner of a common man addressing a common woman. She says that if Ravana touched her body it was not by her choice, and that a person's own conduct is what belongs to them, not what is done to them. She points out that he knew her, was married to her when she was a child, has lived beside her for years, and is now discarding that knowledge because of what others may say. And she makes the point that lands hardest: if you were going to reject me, you should have sent word by Hanuman when he found me. I would have ended my life then, and this whole army need not have crossed the ocean.

Then she turns to Lakshmana and asks him to build her a pyre. He builds it, in silence, looking at his brother's face for a sign, and there is no sign. She walks round Rama once — the circuit one makes around what is holy — and speaks to Agni, and steps into the fire.

And Agni rises out of it with her in his hands, unharmed, and gives her back to Rama with a formal testimony: she is without sin, she has never once in word or thought or glance turned from you, take her.

Rama's answer is that he knew all along. He says the ordeal was necessary not for his own satisfaction but so that the three worlds could see it; that if he had taken her back without proof, people would have called him a fool ruled by desire; and that he could no more give her up than a man could give up his own reputation.

It is at exactly this moment that the gods arrive and Brahma tells Rama that he is Vishnu, and Dasharatha appears in the sky to bless them. Several scholars have observed that the fire ordeal and the theophany are structurally interlocked — the crisis is what brings the gods down — and have taken this as a sign that both belong to the same layer of composition. That is an argument about the text's history. It is not, by itself, an answer to anything Sita said.
And Then, in Book Seven, It Happens Again

We have already seen the second act. Years later, in Ayodhya, a washerman's insult becomes a rumour, and Rama — who states in the same breath that he knows she is innocent — has his pregnant wife taken across the Ganga on a false pretext and left there, with instructions that she not be told until it is too late to refuse.

The difference between the two episodes matters. In Book Six, Rama at least claims a public reason connected to his own honour and offers a proof procedure. In Book Seven he acts on the reported speech of a man he has never met, against a wife whose innocence he has personally certified, and forbids his brothers to argue. It is worse in every respect, and it is the one that ends with her in the ground.
How the Tradition Has Read This

The tradition did not sit comfortably with these passages. Almost everything it did with them can be described as an attempt to make them survivable, and the attempts are ingenious, sincere, and worth knowing in detail.

items: The shadow Sita. The most radical solution: the woman Ravana abducted was never Sita at all. Before the golden deer, Rama secretly asks the real Sita to enter the fire and leave an illusory double in her place; Ravana carries off the double; and the agni-parīkṣā is therefore not a test but a retrieval — the moment the true Sita comes back out of Agni's keeping, where she has been safe all along. This device appears in the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa and is taken up by Tulsidas, which means it is the version tens of millions of north Indians have actually received. It dissolves the problem completely. It also, if you look at it directly, concedes the problem entirely: you do not build a machine this elaborate unless something needs fixing.

Kamban's solution. In the Tamil telling, Ravana does not touch Sita even to abduct her. He digs out the ground she is standing on and carries away the earth with her on it. Same instinct, different engineering.

The fire as evidence, not trial. On the older reading, Sita is not being tested by an authority; she is invoking one. The chastity of a pativratā is understood in this literature as an accumulated power capable of physical effect — the same power by which a wronged woman elsewhere in Indian literature can burn a city down. Sita commands the fire; it does not judge her. On this reading the scene is a demonstration of her strength, not of her subordination, and the person humiliated is Rama.

The king's dilemma. The classical defence: a king rules by consent and reputation, and a ruler whose household is a subject of gossip cannot govern. Rama sacrifices his own happiness — he never remarries, he performs the horse sacrifice beside a golden statue of her, he is visibly destroyed for the rest of the book — to an office that demands he be above suspicion. Note that this defence works only if you accept that the reputation of a government is worth more than the life of the woman inside it. The tradition largely did accept that. You may not.

Tulsidas simply stops. The Ramcharitmanas does not narrate the banishment at all. Its seventh book is about the reign, and Sita is not sent away. The most widely read Ramayana in the Hindi-speaking world solves the Uttara Kanda by declining to have one.

blocks.html: How It Has Been Criticised
The first thing to know is that the criticism is not modern, not foreign, and not secular in origin. It begins inside the Sanskrit tradition, within a few centuries of the text.

blocks.tag: Historical Lens · Bhavabhuti's Protest

blocks.html: Around the eighth century, the playwright Bhavabhūti wrote the Uttararāmacarita — "The Later Deeds of Rama" — a full-length Sanskrit drama that takes the banishment as its entire subject. It is one of the most admired plays in the language, and it is, from beginning to end, about Rama's remorse.

Bhavabhuti does not defend the act. He puts his hero through it and then makes him live with it in front of the audience for five acts — grief-stricken, self-accusing, revisiting the places where they were happy. And at the end he does what the epic would not: he reunites them.

That is a Sanskrit poet, in a fully orthodox literary culture, deciding that the received ending was intolerable and writing a different one. Whatever else is true about the criticism of this episode, "nobody objected until modern feminists came along" is not.

The modern criticism adds several things to Bhavabhuti's. That Sita's innocence is never in doubt within the story, which means the text is not exploring a genuine uncertainty but enacting a norm. That she is asked to prove herself twice and the second demand comes after she has already passed the first, which is what makes it a structure rather than an incident. That the epic's enormous prestige has meant this structure was not merely described but exported — invoked in households, in sermons, in courtrooms, as a model of what a wife owes. And that when a text is used that way, "it is only a story" stops being an available defence.

There is also a reading, common in feminist retellings and in the folk traditions we will come to in Part Four, that gives Sita the last word rather than treating her as the victim of it: that her final act is not despair but judgement. She is asked, in front of an assembly, to perform her innocence again. She declines. She takes the earth's hand instead of Rama's, in public, and goes — and the man left standing there spends the remainder of the poem trying to get her back and failing. Under this reading, the Uttara Kanda is not the story of a woman destroyed. It is the story of a king who is finally refused.
The Argument About Layers, Used Honestly
Now the thing that must be said carefully, because it is the single most common move in this whole debate and it is made dishonestly by both sides.

It is true, and it is the mainstream scholarly position, that the Uttara Kanda — and therefore the banishment — belongs to a later stratum of the text than the core narrative of Books Two to Six. That is not a defensive invention; the arguments for it are set out earlier in this course and they are independent of anything to do with Sita.
But watch what happens when that observation is deployed as a solution, because four things go wrong.

items: It does not touch Book Six. The fire ordeal, the speech about lineage and honour, the list of men Sita might go to instead — all of that is in the war book, which is core by everyone's reckoning. Removing Book Seven leaves the first rejection exactly where it was.

"Later" is not "recent." The Uttara Kanda is present in every complete manuscript tradition, north and south. It has been part of the Ramayana for something on the order of two thousand years. A passage that has been in a text since before most of the world's living religions had scriptures is not an intruder to be shown the door.

Textual history is not moral hygiene. Establishing when a passage entered a text tells you about composition. It tells you nothing about whether the passage is good, and nothing about the effects it has had on the people who received it. A great many women have been told to be like Sita by people who had no idea what a recension is.

And the same move is abused in the other direction. Critics use "it's all a later Brahminical interpolation" to dismiss whatever they dislike, exactly as apologists use it to keep whatever they like. Both are the same manoeuvre: treating philology as a magic wand that removes inconvenient text. It is not one. It is a description of how a book grew.

blocks.html: So the honest statement is this, and it is longer than a slogan because the truth here does not fit in one. The banishment is a later stratum of the poem. It has nevertheless been part of the poem for two millennia and is what most people have received. The rejection at the end of the war is not later and cannot be relocated. The tradition itself found all of this hard, and said so, in Sanskrit, in the eighth century. And Sita's own answer — that what was done to her is not hers, and that a man who knows her should not need the world's permission to say so — is in the text, in her mouth, and has been available to every reader for two thousand years.

blocks.tag: Reflect

blocks.html: One question, and it is not rhetorical. When you find a passage in a text you value that you believe to be wrong, what do you do with it?

There are four moves available, and every tradition on earth uses all four: reinterpret it, attribute it to a later hand, subordinate it to a higher principle in the same text, or simply say that it is wrong and keep the rest. The Ramayana's own history contains examples of all four, executed by people of great seriousness. Whichever you choose, choose it knowingly — and notice that the fourth one, which sounds the most destructive, is the only one that does not require you to misdescribe what is on the page.

sections.label: Question 02 · The Arrow
sections.title: Vali
sections.subtitle: A king shot from concealment, the objection he raises, the answer he is given, and a judgement left to you

blocks.html: There is a temptation, when defending a beloved text, to say that its critics have invented objections that are not really there. On this episode that defence is unavailable, and the reason is simple and should be stated at the front: the objection to Rama's conduct here was written by Valmiki. Nobody had to supply it. The poem stops the battle, gives the dying man a long speech, and lets him make his case.
The Charge
Vali lies on the ground with an arrow in his chest, and what he says amounts to a five-count indictment.

items: There is no quarrel between us. I have not taken your kingdom, insulted you, injured you, entered your country or harmed your people. You and I have never met.
I am not game. I am a forest creature living on fruit and roots. My flesh is not eaten by men like you; my skin and hair are of no use to you. There is no hunter's purpose in my death.
You fought me while I was fighting someone else — engaged, unarmed against you, not looking at you, from behind cover. That is not how a kshatriya kills.

You are wearing dharma as a disguise. The world calls you righteous, and I believed it — that is precisely why I did not take my wife's warning seriously and did not think I needed to fear you. You are a covered well, hidden under grass.

And it was unnecessary. If you had simply told me what you wanted, I would have brought Ravana to you bound, in a single day, and put Sita back in your hands. You had a better option and you took this one.

blocks.html: The fifth point is the sharpest, and it is rarely quoted. Vali is not only accusing Rama of a foul killing. He is pointing out that the entire alliance with Sugriva — the delay, the monsoon, the war — was avoidable.
The Answer
Rama's reply is long, and it is worth setting out as the separate arguments it actually contains, because they do not all point the same way.

items: Jurisdiction. This whole earth, with its forests and hills, belongs to the Ikshvaku line; Bharata now rules it; and those who act within a king's territory are subject to that king's justice. I am not a private party. I am the instrument of a legitimate authority.

The offence. You have taken Ruma, your younger brother's wife, and kept her while he lives. In dharma a younger brother's wife stands in the place of a daughter. The prescribed penalty for what you have done is death.
Punishment purifies. A wrongdoer punished by a king is cleansed and goes upward; one who escapes punishment carries the offence with him. Therefore, Rama says, I have done you a service.

You are an animal. Men lawfully hunt with snares, nets, pits, and concealed shots; they take beasts that are heedless, or turned away, or running. Nothing in the rules of hunting requires that a beast be given notice. You are a vanara.
And I had promised. I gave Sugriva my word before a fire. A promise binds.

blocks.html: Vali accepts it. He says he has no answer, asks Rama to look after his son Angada, asks that Tara not be blamed for anything, and dies reconciled.
What a Careful Reader Notices
I said I would let you judge, and I will. But judging requires seeing the whole board, so here are the observations that any attentive reader — devotee or critic — tends to arrive at.

Two of Rama's arguments cannot both be true. If Vali is a subject of the Ikshvaku realm, liable to punishment under dharma for an offence in family law, then he is a person and not game, and the hunting analogy does not apply to him. If he is a beast, lawfully taken from cover, then he is not a moral subject and cannot be executed for adultery. Rama uses both. Commentators have worked very hard on this, and the working is worth reading, but the tension is real and it is not manufactured by hostile critics.
The standard is not applied evenly. Vali's capital offence is taking his brother's wife. After Vali's death, Tara — Vali's wife — becomes Sugriva's. Rama does not remark on it.

The concession proves nothing. Vali's acceptance is often produced as though it settled the matter: the victim himself was satisfied. But the same poet wrote the objection and the acceptance. An author who allows his hero to be accused and then has the accuser withdraw is showing you the shape of an anxiety, not resolving it.

And the poem has already used this image. A creature shot from concealment while absorbed in something else, by someone it never saw. That is the scene the Ramayana opens with, and the arrow in the first sarga produced the first line of Sanskrit poetry.

blocks.tag: Historical Lens · What Other Tellings Did About It

blocks.html: The surest measure of how uncomfortable an episode is, is how much later effort goes into repairing it. On this one, the effort has been considerable.

A boon is supplied. In many later and popular tellings Vali possesses a boon by which half the strength of any opponent who faces him passes to him, making a fair fight literally impossible and the shot from cover the only available method. It is an elegant fix. It is not part of Valmiki's account of the killing, and its wide circulation is evidence of a felt need rather than of a text.

Tulsidas answers differently. In the Ramcharitmanas, Rama's reply to Vali leans almost entirely on the family-law argument, stated as a general maxim — that a younger brother's wife, a sister, a daughter-in-law and a daughter are the same category, and that looking on them with desire forfeits the offender's life — and drops most of the hunting analogy.

Bhakti reframes it. In the devotional traditions the killing becomes a grace: Vali dies looking at Rama, is granted liberation on the spot, and receives in one moment what austerity could not have earned him. Whether that is a resolution or a change of subject is a judgement each reader has to make.
The Jains delete it. In Vimalasūri's telling the episode does not arise at all: Vālin abdicates in favour of his brother and becomes an ascetic. There is no ambush because there is no killing.

So: your judgement. I will only note what the shape of the material asks of you. This is a hero who behaves badly, in a text that knows it, that stages the accusation at length, and that then supplies a defence which does not entirely hold together. Traditions that treat their heroes as beyond examination do not write scenes like this one. Whatever verdict you reach about Rama, reach a generous one about the poem, which put the case for the prosecution into the record and left it there for two thousand years.

sections.label: Question 03 · The Sword
sections.title: Shambuka
sections.subtitle: Four chapters in the seventh book, and why they have made this poem a political battlefield for a century and a half

blocks.html: This section is a report. I am going to set out what the passage says, what is known about its place in the text, and what a specific tradition of criticism has made of it — accurately, in the terms its own authors use. I am not going to endorse that criticism and I am not going to dismiss it. On this episode, more than any other in Indian literature, the honest thing a teacher can do is make sure you know exactly what is being argued about before you decide what you think.
What the Passage Says

blocks.tag: Scriptural Lens · Uttara Kāṇḍa, sargas 73–76

blocks.html: A brahmin arrives at the palace gate carrying the body of his young son and lays it down in front of the king. He says the boy has died before his time, that untimely death does not occur in a well-governed kingdom, and that therefore this death is the king's fault: there is some defect in Rama's rule, and the child is the evidence.

Rama assembles his advisers. Narada explains the mechanism. In the first age only brahmins performed austerities; in the second, kshatriyas were admitted to it; in the third, vaishyas; and only in the last age may shudras do so. This is the second age. Somewhere in the kingdom a shudra is performing tapas, and that irregularity is what has killed the boy. Find him, Narada says, and the child will live.

Rama takes the Pushpaka and searches in every direction. In the south, by a lake, he finds a man suspended upside down, practising severe austerity. He addresses him and asks — the poem gives the question directly — whether he is a brahmin, a kshatriya, a vaishya or a shudra, and tells him to answer truthfully.

The man answers without fear and, the text says, with pleasure. He gives his name — Śambūka — says he was born of a shudra womb, and says what he is doing it for: he intends to attain the condition of a god, in this body, by austerity.
Rama draws his sword and cuts off his head. The gods, watching, rain down flowers and tell Rama he has done well; the brahmin's son revives at the same moment.

That is the whole episode. Note what it does not contain: Shambuka commits no act of violence, makes no claim on anyone's property, threatens nobody, and is not accused of anything except practising austerity while being what he was born as. He is not given a warning, a hearing, or an alternative. He is asked one question, he answers it honestly, and he is executed for the answer.
Where It Sits in the Text

Everything said earlier in this course about the Uttara Kanda applies here. The seventh book is generally held by scholars to belong to a later stratum than the core narrative of Books Two to Six, for reasons of language, of narrative manner, and of structure — the poem, as we saw, has already concluded once before this book begins.

It is also true, and must be said in the same breath, that the episode is old and firmly transmitted. It is not a marginal note in one manuscript family. By the eighth century it was so well established that Bhavabhūti could build on it: in the second act of the Uttararāmacarita, Rama has killed Shambuka, and Shambuka appears as a celestial being who thanks him, having attained heaven by the king's sword. Whatever the origins of the passage, a major Sanskrit dramatist treated it a thousand-odd years ago as part of the received story and as a benefaction.

That last point cuts in two directions and both should be visible. For a defender it shows the tradition's own reading: Rama's sword is a release, not a punishment. For a critic it shows precisely the mechanism under indictment — a killing described from the top down, with the victim brought back onstage to express gratitude for it.
The Anti-Caste Reading

From the second half of the nineteenth century, this episode became central to a body of Indian social criticism that reads the epics not as devotional literature but as records of a social order — and reads them, deliberately, from the position of those the order subordinates.

Jotirao Phule, in Gulamgiri ("Slavery," 1873), had already proposed a general method: read the myths of divine descent as accounts of conquest, with the gods as invaders and the defeated demons as the indigenous population. That inversion — the demon as the wronged native king — is the seed of much of what follows.

The most sustained and most influential application was by E. V. Ramasamy "Periyar" (1879–1973), the founder of the Self-Respect Movement and the central figure of the Dravidian movement in Tamil Nadu. His reading, set out in the pamphlet published in English as The Ramayana: A True Reading and repeated in decades of speeches, has several distinct parts, and it is worth separating them:

items: Read it literally, and judge it by ordinary morals. Periyar's basic move was to refuse allegorical readings. Take the events as narrated, he said, and ask what you would think of a man who did them: killed from concealment, mutilated a woman who propositioned him, subjected his wife to an ordeal, banished her while pregnant, and beheaded an ascetic for practising austerity.

Ravana as the southern king. On this reading Ravana is a Dravidian sovereign — learned, capable, a ruler of a wealthy and ordered kingdom — and the epic is the account of a northern invasion told by the invaders. Shurpanakha is a woman of that people, disfigured for speaking her desire; Vali is a southern king killed by deceit; the vanaras are the forest peoples of the south, described as animals by the conquerors.

Shambuka as the proof. Of all the episodes, this is the one Periyar returned to most, because it requires no interpretation to make its point. The offence is birth; the penalty is death; the sentence is carried out personally by the king whom the tradition holds up as the standard of righteousness; and the gods applaud.

Therefore, refuse the text publicly. Periyar treated ridicule and public rejection as political instruments. His movement burned images of Rama — most prominently in a campaign in 1971 — as a deliberate act of desacralisation, intended to break the story's authority over people who had been taught to revere it.

blocks.html: B. R. Ambedkar examined the same material in a different register. His essay "The Riddle of Rama and Krishna," part of the manuscript published posthumously as Riddles in Hinduism, goes through Rama's conduct episode by episode, Shambuka among them, and asks how a figure with this record came to be the moral exemplar of a civilisation. When the Government of Maharashtra published the volume in 1987, it produced weeks of demonstrations and counter-demonstrations in the state, and a dispute over whether the government should disown the chapter — which is a reasonable measure of how live this material remains.

There is also a literary tradition of rewriting rather than denouncing. The Kannada poet Kuvempu — a Jnanpith laureate — took up the episode in his play Śūdra Tapasvi (1944), and reworked it so that Rama does not kill the ascetic: the sword is turned aside and the assumptions behind the errand are exposed instead. Doing that in 1944, inside the tradition rather than against it, was its own kind of intervention. Since then, Shambuka has become one of the recurring figures of modern Dalit writing in several Indian languages.
The Replies, Stated Fairly
Defenders of the text make four main arguments, and a reader should know them as well as the criticism.

items: Stratum. The episode is in the seventh book and therefore, on the scholarly consensus, later than the core poem — not part of the earliest Ramayana.

Cosmology, not sociology. On the classical reading the offence is not "a shudra doing something forbidden" as a matter of privilege, but a violation of the ordering of the ages, whose direct physical consequence — a dead child — is stated in the text. Rama is restoring a broken order, not defending a class interest.
Benefit to the victim. As Bhavabhuti has it, and as several commentators hold, Shambuka attains by that death exactly the celestial state he was seeking. The sword is the fulfilment of his austerity.

The epic is not uniform. The same Rama embraces Guha the Nishada chieftain as a brother, eats the food of Shabari, a tribal ascetic woman, performs funeral rites with his own hands for a vulture, and makes his alliance and his closest friendship with forest creatures whom the text's own vocabulary treats as beneath men. Any account of the Ramayana's social vision has to hold those passages and this one at the same time.

blocks.html: And the critics' replies to those replies are equally available: that lateness is a fact about composition and not about consequence, since the passage has been in the received text for two millennia; that a cosmological framing does not alter what is done to the person, and that the text supplies no offence other than birth; that gratitude assigned to a dead man by his killer's tradition is not evidence of anything; and that the warmth Rama shows to Guha and Shabari is the warmth of a superior to devoted inferiors, which is not the thing at issue when someone attempts to rise.

That is the argument. Both sides of it are held by serious people, and it has not been settled by anything I could write here. What this course insists on is only that the passage be reported as it stands — which is what I have done above — and that neither the criticism nor the defence be paraphrased into a straw man before you have looked at the four chapters yourself.

blocks.tag: Reflect

blocks.html: Notice what this episode has in common with the two before it. In each case the poem does something difficult, and in each case the tradition responded — not by hiding it, but by generating readings, rewritings, corrections and rebuttals for two thousand years.

That is worth registering before you move on. A text that produced Bhavabhuti's protest, Kuvempu's refusal, Periyar's demolition and the commentators' patient defences is not a dead monument. It is a place where a civilisation has been arguing with itself in public, at very high volume, for longer than most nations have existed.

sections.label: Question 04 · The Enemy
sections.title: Ravana
sections.subtitle: The scholar, the musician, the devotee of Shiva — and the dignity the poem itself gives him

blocks.html: Every October, across north India, an effigy of Ravana is packed with fireworks and burned in front of a crowd. It is one of the most vivid religious images the subcontinent produces, and it has taught several generations that this is a story with a monster in it. The Sanskrit text is a good deal more interesting than that, and so are large parts of the tradition.
What He Is, in the Text

Start with his descent, which the epic never lets you forget. Ravana is the grandson of Pulastya, one of Brahma's mind-born sons, and the son of the sage Vishrava. He is a brahmin on his father's side and a rakshasa on his mother's. He is learned: master of the Vedas and of the sciences, an accomplished performer of ritual, the sort of adversary who can quote at you. The tradition's gloss on his ten heads reads them as his learning — the four Vedas and the six ancillary disciplines — which is a symbolic reading rather than the epic's own statement, but it tells you what the tradition thought he was made of.

He is a devotee of Shiva, and one particular story is the source of his name. In the Uttara Kanda, Ravana, flying home, is stopped at Mount Kailasa and told the mountain may not be overflown. He puts his arms under it and lifts. Shiva, seated above with Parvati, presses down with the toe of one foot, and Ravana's hands are caught under the weight of the mountain. He roars — a scream that shakes the worlds — and then, trapped, he sings. He sings to Shiva for a very long time, and Shiva, pleased, releases him, gives him the sword Chandrahasa, and gives him the name by which he is known: Rāvaṇa, from the root that means to howl — the one who made the worlds scream, and who screamed.

The musical tradition around him is old and widespread. The Śiva Tāṇḍava Stotra, one of the most rhythmically extraordinary hymns in Sanskrit, is traditionally ascribed to him; images across India show him playing a stringed instrument, sometimes said to be strung from his own sinews; and the bowed folk instrument called the rāvaṇahattā, played in Rajasthan and in Sri Lanka, carries his name.

blocks.html: The Dignity the Poem Gives Him
This is the part that surprises readers who come to the Sanskrit expecting propaganda. Valmiki does not write Ravana as contemptible.

When Hanuman finds him asleep in the fifth book, the description is of a magnificent animal at rest — enormous, marked with old scars from the tusks of Indra's elephant and from Vishnu's discus, breathing like a great snake, surrounded by his sleeping women, and Hanuman stands there and thinks that if this being were not set on unrighteousness he could rule heaven itself. His city is beautiful and the poem says so. His counsellors argue with him and their arguments are good ones. His restraint with Sita, whatever its cause, is a fact of the plot.

And when he is dead, the epic gives him two things. The first is Mandodari's lament, which is a real elegy and which says true things about him. The second is one line from Rama. Vibhishana, still angry, refuses to perform his brother's funeral rites; and Rama overrules him:

blocks.sk:
मरणान्तानि वैराणि निर्वृत्तं नः प्रयोजनम् ।
क्रियतामस्य संस्कारो ममाप्येष यथा तव ॥
