maraṇāntāni vairāṇi nirvṛttaṁ naḥ prayojanam |
kriyatām asya saṁskāro mamāpy eṣa yathā tava ||
blocks.mn: "Enmities end at death. Our purpose here is finished. Let his rites be performed — he is as much mine now as he is yours."
blocks.src: — Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, Yuddha Kāṇḍa, sarga 109 (numbering varies)

blocks.html: Maraṇāntāni vairāṇi. Four syllables and a verdict. It is one of the most quoted lines in Indian moral discourse, and it is said over the body of the poem's chief villain by the man who has just killed him.
Where He Is Not the Villain

items: The Jain tellings. In Vimalasūri's Paümacariya and the tradition that follows it, Ravana is a vidyādhara — not a demon at all, but a member of a high class of beings with mastery of magical sciences. He is a noble king, a Jain layman, brought down by one attachment he cannot govern. He is killed not by Rama but by Lakshmana. And Jain tradition holds that he is destined to be reborn as a Tīrthaṅkara. He is not evil; he is a tragedy about desire.

Kamban's Tamil telling. Ravana is given grandeur and interiority — a king who knows what he is doing to himself and cannot stop, and whose refusal to touch Sita is presented as a kind of terrible fidelity.

Sri Lanka. Ravana has a long life in Sinhala tradition as an ancient king of the island, and in recent decades has become the centre of a substantial popular revival, with claimed sites and a body of writing about him as a founder-figure of Lankan civilisation. Historians treat most of that material with caution; its cultural energy is nevertheless real.

The Dravidian reading. As set out in the previous section: Ravana as the learned southern sovereign and the epic as the conquerors' account. Whatever one makes of it as history, it has been one of the most politically consequential readings of any text in modern India.

And parts of India venerate him. Bisrakh in Uttar Pradesh is held locally to be his birthplace and does not celebrate his burning. There is a temple to him at Kanpur that opens its doors once a year, on Dussehra — the day everyone else is burning him. Mandsaur in Madhya Pradesh treats him as a son-in-law of the town, Mandodari being claimed as a local daughter. Certain brahmin communities claim descent from him and perform rites for him rather than fireworks.

blocks.tag: Symbolic Lens · Why the Villain Had to Be Great

blocks.html: The tradition's own explanation of Ravana's stature is theological and it is worth hearing. In the Vaishnava reading, an incarnation of Vishnu does not descend to swat an insect. The scale of the adversary is the measure of the descent, and so Ravana must be learned, powerful, devout, and very nearly right — otherwise there is nothing for a god to come down for.

There is a further move in some Puranic traditions: that Ravana is a gatekeeper of Vishnu's own heaven, cursed to be born as an enemy three times over, and that his hostility is itself a form of relation — that to be destroyed by God, having thought about nothing but God for a lifetime of hatred, is a kind of arrival. It is not the reading you get from Valmiki. It is a reading that a devotional tradition produced because it could not bear to let its greatest enemy be merely an enemy.

sections.label: Chapter 15 · The Family
sections.title: The Many Ramayanas
sections.subtitle: Pali, Prakrit, Tamil, Awadhi, Bengali, Telugu, Assamese, Malayalam, Thai, Javanese — and what each one moves

blocks.html: We began with Ramanujan's proposition, and now we can test it against the evidence. Below is a small sample of the family — a dozen tellings out of hundreds. Read the last column first. In every case, the change is not decorative: it is the point of that telling's existence.

head: Telling
Language
Date
One thing it changes
rows: Layered; roughly 5th–4th c. BCE to 3rd c. CE

The baseline against which the others are usually measured — though not the source of all of them. In its core books Rama is treated overwhelmingly as a man; the explicit theology sits in the outer two.
Within the Jātaka collection; commentarial recension c. 5th c. CE, older material behind it

Sita is Rama's sister, and afterwards his queen — a convention of royal marriage the story takes for granted. There is no Ravana, no abduction and no war. Rama is the Bodhisatta, and the moral is equanimity: told of his father's death, he does not grieve, and explains why.
Claims the 1st c. CE; usually placed c. 3rd–5th c. CE

Ravana is a noble vidyādhara — not a demon but a king of a class of beings with mastery of the magical sciences, a Jain layman brought down by one ungoverned attachment. And Lakshmana, not Rama, kills him, and takes the karmic consequence. Rama does no killing and attains liberation. The text presents itself as a correction of a false and slanderous account.

Adapted principally from the Sanskrit Bhaṭṭikāvya rather than from Valmiki directly. In the Javanese and Balinese performance tradition that grew from it, the punakawan — indigenous clown-servants with no Indian counterpart — walk into the story and stay.
Devotion from the first line: Rama is God, unambiguously. Ravana is given tragic interiority. And Ravana never touches Sita — he digs out the ground she is standing on and carries away the earth.
Among the earliest complete Ramayanas in any modern Indian language. Kandali deliberately domesticates the register — kings and sages speak like Assamese villagers — and says so.

Rewrites the whole epic as Advaita Vedanta: Rama is Brahman and knows it throughout, and the narrative becomes an instruction in non-duality. Introduces the shadow Sita, hidden in fire before the abduction.

Adds Rama's out-of-season worship of Durga before the final battle — the akāl bodhan, the awakening of the goddess at the wrong time of year, which is the mythic charter for Bengal's autumn Durga Puja.
14th c.; attributed to Gona Budda Reddy

Composed in dvipada, a plain couplet metre made for singing rather than learned recitation — a deliberate move out of the scholar's hands. It takes in a body of folk episodes with no counterpart in Valmiki.

The most widely recited Ramayana on earth. Rama is God without remainder and the poem is an act of worship rather than a narrative. It takes over the shadow Sita — and it does not narrate the banishment at all.
The whole poem is narrated by a parrot — the kiḷippāṭṭu or "parrot-song" form. It follows the Adhyatma Ramayana's theology and is one of the foundation stones of modern Malayalam.
Standard version composed under Rama I, 1797 (older tellings lost)

Hanuman is not celibate — he is a worldly, amorous, mischievous warrior. Thotsakan (Ravana) receives a full royal biography and real sympathy. And the story is naturalised as national history: the capital was Ayutthaya, and Thai kings are styled Rama to this day.

blocks.html: What the Table Shows

Look at what is being moved. Whether Rama is a man, a Bodhisatta, or God. Whether Ravana is a demon, a tragic king, or a Jain nobleman. Who kills him. Whether Sita is a wife, a sister, or a projection. Whether the abduction physically happens. Whether the banishment exists. These are not variant readings of a line — they are different answers to what the story is for.

And the direction of borrowing is not a simple tree. Ramanujan's five examples in the essay we began with — Valmiki, Kamban, Vimalasuri, the Thai Ramakien and a Kannada folk telling — were chosen precisely to show that you cannot line them up as parent and children. His image for the field was a shared pool of names, incidents, images and situations, like a lexicon, from which each poet composes a new sentence. Some tellings are close translations. Some are arguments. Some are refutations that assume you already know the version they are attacking.

The geographical spread is the other half of the evidence, and it is easy to underrate from inside India. There are living Rama traditions in Cambodia (the Reamker), Myanmar (the Yama Zatdaw), Laos (Phra Lak Phra Lam), the Malay world (the Hikayat Seri Rama), Bali, and among Tibetan and Central Asian communities. In much of Southeast Asia these are not imported curiosities: they are the local classical repertoire — the wall paintings of a national temple, the shadow-puppet cycle, the court dance form.

blocks.tag: Historical Lens · The Newest Telling

blocks.html: The most consequential Ramayana of the last century was made for television. Ramanand Sagar's Ramayan, broadcast on Doordarshan in 1987–88, drew audiences estimated in the tens of millions and produced the widely reported phenomenon of streets emptying on Sunday mornings, sets garlanded, screens treated as shrines.

It is a telling like any other, with its own choices: it draws heavily on Tulsidas rather than Valmiki, and where it selects and smooths it does so in a particular direction. Its effect on which version of the story most Indians now carry in their heads is difficult to overstate — and it arrived precisely in the years when the Ramayana was becoming a central object in Indian public politics.

A tradition of three hundred tellings acquired, in a single decade, one telling with a distribution advantage none of the others ever had. That is a genuinely new thing in this story's history, and it is worth watching carefully.

sections.label: Chapter 16 · The Songs
sections.title: The Ramayanas Women Sing
sections.subtitle: Where the Sanskrit is silent, the songs are loudest — and they are almost all about Sita

blocks.html: There is a whole layer of this tradition that no manuscript catalogue records, because it was never written down: the Ramayana as sung by women, at home, at weddings, during pregnancy, while grinding grain, in the languages people actually speak. It has been collected seriously only in the last century or so, and what it contains changes the shape of the whole subject.

The first thing to notice is where the songs go. They concentrate almost exactly on the places where the Sanskrit is thinnest: the wedding, the household, pregnancy and childbirth, the relations between women, and the exile. The great battles are barely there. Hanuman's leap is barely there. What the songs want is the part of the story that happens indoors.
Telugu Songs

The scholar Velcheru Narayana Rao collected and analysed a body of Telugu women's songs in an essay titled — pointedly — "A Ramayana of Their Own: Women's Oral Tradition in Telugu," published in Paula Richman's Many Rāmāyaṇas (1991), the same volume that carries Ramanujan's essay.

These are domestic songs, sung at the rituals women run. In them Sita is the centre and the subject; Rama is often a peripheral figure and not an especially impressive one — an ordinary husband, sometimes petty, sometimes badly advised, viewed the way a bride's family views a son-in-law who has not behaved well. The songs treat the epic's crises as household matters: what a mother-in-law said, who was jealous of whom, what a pregnant woman craved, how a daughter was treated when she was sent back.
Mithila

In the Maithili-speaking region on either side of the India–Nepal border — the country of Janaka, where the Sita of the story was raised — she is not primarily a symbol. She is a local daughter married out of the district.

The wedding repertoire there includes gālī, songs of ritual abuse directed at the groom's party, and they are not suspended for this particular groom: Rama's family gets its share on the day. And the tone of the region's later songs about her is the tone of a family whose daughter was treated badly by the people she was sent to live with. It is a shift of point of view that no amount of commentary produces, and it comes simply from singing the story from the house she left rather than the house she entered.
Women Who Wrote

items: Chandrabati, sixteenth-century Bengal, composed a Ramayana that stays with Sita — her birth, her marriage, her exile, her abandonment — and gives her a bāromāsī, the twelve-month song in which a woman tells her sorrow month by month through the turning year. It is unfinished, and it comes down to us through the folk-ballad collections of eastern Bengal rather than through any scholarly line of transmission.

Molla (Ātukūri Molla), around the same period in the Telugu country, a potter's daughter who wrote a Ramayana in plain, singable Telugu and said openly that she had no formal training in the learned conventions. That statement is itself part of the poem's argument.

Volga (P. Lalita Kumari), in the Telugu novella cycle Vimukta — translated as The Liberation of Sita, and awarded the Sahitya Akademi Prize in 2015 — sends Sita, after the banishment, to meet the other women the epic used and set aside, and lets them talk.

Ranganayakamma, also in Telugu, produced in the 1970s a full-length Marxist critique under a title that translates as Ramayana: The Poisonous Tree — a very different project, and evidence of how wide the range of women's engagement with this text has been.

blocks.tag: Story · Whose Daughter Was She?

blocks.html: One motif that turns up repeatedly in the folk and Jain traditions, and in parts of Southeast Asia, deserves its own mention: Sita is Ravana's daughter. In these tellings she is born to him, a prophecy says she will destroy him, she is set adrift or buried, and Janaka finds her in the furrow.

Ramanujan draws attention to this motif in the essay we began with, and once you see it the whole architecture of the story rearranges: the abduction becomes a father reclaiming a child he does not recognise, the war becomes a family destroying itself, and the prophecy comes true exactly because of the measures taken to prevent it.
It is not Valmiki. It is also not a mistake, or a degraded copy. It is a different telling, held by real communities, doing something the Sanskrit does not do.

The last thing to say about this layer is the most important, and it is easy to miss. These songs are not a rejection of the Ramayana. Nobody in them is refusing the story or standing outside it. They are sung by women who revere it, at religious occasions, in the middle of lives arranged by it — and they are the same women who were held up as Sita's imitators. Given the story and told to be like her, they sang her from the inside, and what came out was not obedience. It was commentary.

sections.label: Chapter 17 · Evidence
sections.title: What Science Actually Says
sections.subtitle: The claims made about the Ramayana, tested — corroborated, open, and contradicted

blocks.html: Every course in this library ends here. For sixteen chapters we have been inside the material: what the poem says, how it grew, what it has been made to mean. Now we step outside and ask a different question in a different voice. What can actually be shown?

Three rules, and then the verdicts. Name the finding — "scientists have proved" is a rumour about evidence, not evidence. "No evidence for" is not "evidence against" — collapsing those two is the commonest dishonesty in this territory, and sceptics commit it as often as enthusiasts. And nothing here needs to win: if a claim fails it fails, and the Ramayana is not diminished by a sandbank being a sandbank.
The Verdicts

items.claim: The Ramayana exists in hundreds of distinct tellings across a dozen languages and cultures, and its regional variation is documented rather than speculative.
items.html: This is not a thesis; it is a shelf. The Belgian-Indian scholar Camille Bulcke, in his survey Rāmakathā, tallied on the order of three hundred separate tellings — the count A. K. Ramanujan took for the title of "Three Hundred Rāmāyaṇas" (1987), collected in Paula Richman's Many Rāmāyaṇas (University of California Press, 1991) and followed by her Questioning Ramayanas (2001). Every item in the table in Part Four is a printed, catalogued, translatable text or a living performance tradition: Pali, Prakrit, Tamil, Awadhi, Bengali, Telugu, Assamese, Malayalam, Old Javanese, Thai, Khmer, Burmese, Lao, Malay. Within Sanskrit alone the variation is measurable: the Baroda Critical Edition (1960–1975) was constituted by collating manuscripts from every region, and its apparatus prints, verse by verse, where the Northern and Southern recensions diverge. The limits: "three hundred" is a scholar's tally, not a census, and the number depends entirely on what you count as a distinct telling. What is solid is the fact of plurality and the impossibility of deriving all of it from one parent text.

items.claim: Ayodhya, Mithila and Kishkindha are real places with long, continuous human settlement.
items.html: Ayodhya sits on the Sarayu in eastern Uttar Pradesh and is one of the oldest continuously inhabited towns in the Ganga plain; it appears in early Buddhist and Jain literature under the name Sāketa, and excavation — including the "Archaeology of the Ramayana Sites" project directed by B. B. Lal in the 1970s and later work by the Archaeological Survey of India — has recovered occupation levels going back into the first millennium BCE, with the Northern Black Polished Ware horizon well represented. Mithila is a real region straddling north Bihar and the Nepal Tarai, with Janakpur as its traditional centre and a living pilgrimage economy. Kishkindha is identified with the Tungabhadra country around Hampi in Karnataka, a landscape saturated with Ramayana place-names — Anjanadri, Rishyamukha, Pampa — long before Vijayanagara was built there. The limits, and they matter. That the geography is real establishes that the poem is set in a world its composers knew; it does not establish that the events occurred, any more than the existence of Troy establishes Achilles. The Hampi identification is a continuous tradition, not an archaeological demonstration. And Ayodhya's excavation history has been the subject of a long legal and political dispute in India concerning a particular site's later structural sequence; that dispute is about something other than the epic, and this course takes no position on it.

items.claim: The core poem can be dated.
items.html: Genuinely open, and open at both ends. There is no external anchor — no inscription, no dated manuscript from anywhere near the period, nothing to peg the text to. Everything comes from internal evidence: the state of the language, metrical development, the material culture the poem knows, the geography it can name, and its relations to other datable literature. The conventional working range puts the earliest stages of the core somewhere around the fifth to fourth century BCE and the layered whole reaching roughly its present shape by about the third century CE — the stratification argued in detail by John Brockington in Righteous Rāma (1984) and The Sanskrit Epics (1998). Individual passages can sometimes be placed relative to others: the direction-lists in Book Four name Yavanas and Śakas, peoples whose names enter Indian usage only after contact with Greeks and Central Asians, which marks those passages as late — while saying nothing about the core. Serious scholars argue for an earlier beginning and for a later completion. What is not available, from anyone, is a year. Anyone offering you one is selling something.

items.claim: A historical figure lies behind Rama.
items.html: Unresolved, and probably permanently so. There is no evidence either way, and the two halves of that sentence carry equal weight. No inscription names him; no coin, no contemporary record, no archaeological horizon corresponds to the events. But notice what kind of absence that is: writing is not attested in India after the Indus script until the third century BCE, so a king of a small Iron Age polity in the eastern Ganga plain — which is what the poem describes — could not have left an epigraphic trace of the kind that would settle this. The Ikshvaku dynasty is a real lineage in Indian tradition; Ayodhya is a real and ancient town; the poem's political world of modest neighbouring kingdoms is broadly consistent with a real period. None of which is evidence for a person. The plausibility of a setting is not the historicity of a character. The honest verdict is the uncomfortable one: absence of evidence here is not evidence of absence, and it is also not evidence of presence, and no responsible person should convert it into either.

items.claim: Adam's Bridge / Rāma Setu is an engineered structure — a causeway built by human or superhuman agency.
items.html:
The formation is real and is exactly where the poem says a crossing was: a chain of shoals, sandbanks, coral and calcareous sandstone running some forty-eight kilometres in shallow water between Rameswaram on the Indian side and Mannar Island off Sri Lanka. The geological consensus is that it is natural. It sits on a shallow submerged ridge between two land masses that were joined during low sea-level stands, and its surface features are the ordinary products of coastal processes: longshore sediment transport, sand spits growing and coalescing, coral colonising warm shallow water. Marine sediment work and remote-sensing studies, including by the Geological Survey of India, describe it in these terms. Published age estimates for the various components differ from one another and run to many thousands of years for the shoals and vastly longer for the ridge beneath — that is, the feature substantially predates any date anyone proposes for the epic, and shows no single episode of construction, which is precisely what a built causeway would require. On the satellite images circulated online as proof: NASA has stated publicly that imagery of this kind cannot determine whether a formation is natural or artificial, and the images were never evidence of anything. (In 2007, in litigation over the Sethusamudram canal project, the Archaeological Survey of India filed an affidavit stating there was no scientific evidence for the structure being man-made; after large public protest the affidavit was withdrawn. That is a fact about a controversy, not about geology.)

And now the part that matters more than the geology. None of the above has any bearing whatsoever on what that place means to the people who venerate it. Rameswaram is one of the great pilgrimage centres of India, a jyotirlinga and one of the four dhāms; the tradition there holds that Rama himself established the linga after the war. Millions of people have walked to that shore because of this poem, and a sedimentological finding about how sand moves has no authority over any of it. Geology can tell you how a bank of sand came to be in the Palk Strait. It cannot tell you what it is to stand there. Keeping those two statements apart, without letting either one bully the other, is the entire purpose of the three lenses.

items.claim: The Ramayana describes nuclear weapons, and the Puṣpaka was an aircraft.
items.html: This reads modern technology into figurative Sanskrit, and it does so by ignoring how the text actually behaves. The astras are not devices: they are invoked by mantra, named for the deities who own them, given and withdrawn by teachers, and dismissed by name — and they are described in the standard poetic vocabulary of fire, wind, light and thunder that this literature applies to everything impressive, including sunrise and anger. The Puṣpaka is a flying palace of gold that goes where its owner wishes, expands to hold any number of passengers, and is won and lost as spoil; it has an owner and a history, but no mechanism, no fuel and no pilot. It is a magical vehicle in a literature densely populated with them. The specifics that get quoted usually are not even from this epic — the "nuclear" passages are generally lifted from the Mahabharata, and the Oppenheimer quotation everyone repeats is Bhagavad Gītā 11.32, a theological statement about time with no technological content. The "ancient aircraft" literature traces largely to the Vaimānika Śāstra, presented as ancient but produced through the mediumistic dictation of Pandit Subbaraya Shastry in about 1918–1923 and first published in 1952; in 1974 a team of aeronautical engineers at the Indian Institute of Science — H. S. Mukunda, S. M. Deshpande, H. R. Nagendra, A. Prabhu and S. P. Govindaraju — published a technical assessment concluding that the craft described could not fly and that the text shows no grasp of aeronautics. The claim about radioactive skeletons at Mohenjo-daro has no basis in any excavation report. The deepest objection to this genre is not that it is false but that it is a surrender: it concedes that a poem is worthless unless it turns out to be an engineering manual, which is a proposition no one who loves the Ramayana should accept for a moment.

items.claim: Planetarium software applied to the poem's verses yields the date of Rama's birth.
items.html: Books and websites in this genre — the best known being Pushkar Bhatnagar's Dating the Era of Lord Rama, which arrives at a day in January 5114 BCE — feed the astrological configurations mentioned in the Bala Kanda into sky-simulation software and report a match. The method fails at three separate points. The verses are not observational records: they give auspicious positions in conventional astrological language, of the kind used to dignify any royal birth. The text is layered, and the birth passages sit in the book most scholars judge latest. And a search across many thousands of years against loose constraints will always return hits, which is why different practitioners of this method produce dates differing from one another by centuries and millennia. A result that cannot fail is not a measurement.

blocks.tag: Symbolic Lens · Why the Setu Item Is the Whole Course

blocks.html: If you take one thing from this chapter, take the shape of that fifth verdict, because it is the model for everything difficult.

Two statements, both true, neither cancelling the other. The chain of shoals in the Palk Strait formed by natural coastal processes over a very long time. That shore is one of the holiest places in India and this poem is the reason. A person who cannot hold both of those at once will end up either lying about the sediment or sneering at the pilgrims, and there is no third failure mode.

The lenses are not a diplomatic device for avoiding offence. They are an accuracy technique. The sentence "the setu is natural" is a claim in one column; the sentence "the setu is sacred" is a claim in another; and the reason they do not contradict each other is that they are not about the same thing.
At the start I asked you to write down the Ramayana as you were carrying it — where it began, where it ended, what it was finally saying. Find that page now.

I do not know what it says. But I would guess it ended with a coronation, and that Book Seven was thin or absent, and that Sita appeared in it more as a quality than as a person. That is not ignorance. That is what happens when a story is handed to you by people who loved it enough to choose which parts to hand over.
What you have now is not mainly a set of facts. Facts go first. In a year you may not remember which sarga Sita's oath is in, or who Vimalasuri was, or how a sand shoal forms.

What may last is one habit, and it is worth more than the facts. When someone tells you what the Ramayana says, you will now ask, without hostility and almost without thinking: which one? Valmiki or Tulsidas — and if Valmiki, north or south, vulgate or critical edition? Through Book Six, or through Book Seven? The Sanskrit, or the songs the women of your own family sing at weddings? Those are not sceptic's questions. They are the questions of somebody who has actually been in the building.
Three Hundred Is Not a Weakness

There is an instinct, when you learn that a sacred story exists in three hundred versions, to feel that something has been taken from you. I want to leave you with the opposite thought, and I think the evidence is on its side.

A story that can only be told one way has one life, and when the conditions change it dies. This one has been rewritten by people who disagreed with it — by Buddhists who removed the war, by Jains who made the demon a nobleman and gave the killing to somebody else, by a Tamil poet who would not let Ravana touch her, by Bhavabhuti who could not bear the ending and wrote another, by Kuvempu who turned the sword aside, by women at grindstones who sang it from the bride's family's side, by Periyar who burned its hero in public. Every one of those is a load test. The story took the weight each time and is still standing, in more languages than it started with.
That is not dilution. That is what durability looks like from close up. The texts that vanish are the ones nobody was allowed to argue with.
The Bird
Two images to end on, and they are the two ends of this poem.

The first is where it began: a man at a river, watching a hunter kill one of a pair of birds, and finding that something has come out of his mouth that he did not compose — grief with a shape on it. Śoka becoming śloka. Everything that followed, for two and a half thousand years, in every language named in this course, grows out of that one involuntary sentence spoken on behalf of a creature that could not speak for itself.

The second is a scene inside the poem. Two boys who have never met their father are singing his life to him in his own hall, in the metre their teacher invented that morning by the river, and the part they are about to reach is the part where he sends their mother away. The Ramayana's own picture of what a Ramayana is: a retelling, performed by people the story wronged, to the person it is about, who has to sit and listen.

That is what remains. Not a single authorised account with a lesson at the end — a story big enough that everyone who was hurt in it got to sing it back, and a tradition that kept every one of those songs.
The reading ends here. Oṁ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ.
